    The

    Rudement Features Manual

    Operating guide for the added instruments, effects, performance tools, and MIDI functions

    This manual explains how to find and use the Rudement features on the Deluge. Each chapter begins with the controls and gestures, then covers practical behaviour, saved state, and limits that matter while playing.

    00Installing the Firmware
    Synthstrom Deluge · Rudement Firmware
    Chapter 00

    Installing the Firmware

    Back up the card, load the .bin, check the version, and go back

    Loading firmware on the Deluge takes a minute: one file on the SD card and SHIFT held at power-on. Back up the whole card first. Songs saved with this firmware may not open on older firmware, and the backup is your way back.

    SD card root · SHIFT at power-on · SETTINGS → FIRMWARE VERSION · 7SEG: FIRM
    01Before you start: back up the whole SD card
    1. Power the Deluge off and take out the SD card.
    2. Put the card in your computer and copy everything on it into a new folder, for example Deluge backup with today's date. That includes SONGS, SYNTHS, KITS, SAMPLES and SETTINGS, plus any .bin file already in the card's top level.
    3. Keep a copy of the firmware you are running now. If there is no .bin on the card, download your current version from Synthstrom before you go on, so you have something to go back to.
    Why the whole card

    Your songs, kits, synths and samples all live on the card. A song opened and saved with newer firmware may refuse to open on older firmware (the Deluge says Your firmware version is too old to open this file). The untouched copy in your backup is what still opens there.

    02Load the firmware
    1. Download the Rudement firmware. It is a single file ending in .bin.
    2. Copy it to the top level of the SD card, not inside a folder.
    3. Make sure it is the only .bin file in the top level. Move any other one into your backup folder.
    4. Eject the card properly from your computer, then put it back in the Deluge.
    5. Hold SHIFT and switch the Deluge on. Keep holding SHIFT until the Deluge has started up.
    6. The Deluge loads the new firmware and starts normally. If it starts on your old firmware instead, power off and try again, holding SHIFT before you switch on.

    The .bin can stay on the card. It only loads when SHIFT is held at power-on.

    03Check the version

    Open SETTINGS → FIRMWARE VERSION (7-segment: FIRM). It should read 1.3.0-rudement. Then open SETTINGS → COMMUNITY FEATURES and look for the Rudement upgrades folder; chapter 01 lists what is in it.

    04Going back
    1. Power off and put the SD card in your computer.
    2. Move the Rudement .bin off the card, and copy the firmware you want to go back to into the top level. Again, only one .bin there.
    3. If a song will not open on the older firmware, copy that song's file from your backup back into SONGS.
    4. Put the card back, hold SHIFT and switch on, then check SETTINGS → FIRMWARE VERSION.
    Your feature switches are kept

    Community Features choices are saved in SETTINGS/CommunityFeatures.XML on the card. Other firmware keeps the Rudement entries it does not know about, so they are still there if you come back to Rudement later.

    01Community Features
    Synthstrom Deluge · Rudement Firmware
    Chapter 01

    Community Features

    Feature switches and their defaults

    Community Features lets you expose or gate Rudement functions without clearing the settings saved in a song.

    SETTINGS → COMMUNITY FEATURES → Rudement upgrades · 7SEG: RUDE
    01Finding the switches
    1. Open SETTINGS → COMMUNITY FEATURES.
    2. Scroll to Rudement upgrades. A 7-segment Deluge displays RUDE.
    3. Press SELECT to open the folder. The supported Rudement instruments, effects, workflow tools, and MIDI features are listed below.
    4. Select a switch and turn SELECT to choose On or Off.
    Three Rudement switches are outside the folder

    Chord Brush, Keyboard Note Preview, and Retrospective Capture appear directly in SETTINGS → COMMUNITY FEATURES. They are not inside Rudement upgrades. Check both locations when reviewing every Rudement switch.

    02Defaults and effects
    GroupFeature7SEGDefaultWhat the switch controls
    Rudement upgradesKit SplitSPLTOffEnables the command that separates a kit into single-sound kits.
    Rudement upgradesFour-Band EQEQ4OnShows the two added mid bands and their controls.
    Rudement upgradesBouls EngineBOULOnShows Bouls as an Oscillator 1 type.
    Rudement upgradesWisps FXDUSTOnShows Wisps controls in supported contexts.
    Rudement upgradesGristleatorGRISOnShows the Gristleator LFO, two-lane Slicer, and all fourteen controls.
    Rudement upgradesSearSEAROnShows Sear drive and tone controls.
    Rudement upgradesScene CaptureCAPTOffEnables scene capture in Song view.
    Rudement upgradesGrid Column ReorderCOLSOffEnables horizontal track reordering in the grid.
    Rudement upgradesTemp HoldHOLDOffHolds each changed parameter's original value while SHIFT is held, then restores it when SHIFT is released.
    Rudement upgradesTemp Hold TailsTAILOnWhen a hold ends, a delay that was turned up during it rings out instead of stopping dead. Shown only while Temp Hold is On.
    Rudement upgradesMIDI FXMIFXOnShows and enables the MIDI FX pages.
    Rudement upgradesHarmonizeCHRDOffEnables chord-following playback.
    Rudement upgradesStrumSTRMOffEnables timed spreading of simultaneous notes.
    Rudement upgradesDelay FiltersDLYFOffShows and activates the delay feedback HPF and LPF.
    Rudement upgradesVisualizerVISOffChooses the OLED Visualizer's starting mode, or Off. OLED only.
    Rudement upgradesVisualizer PriorityVPRIOffLets the Visualizer keep the screen over popups. Shown only while a Visualizer mode is chosen.
    Rudement upgradesLoop RemixLRMXOffShows and enables the Loop Remix page in MIDI FX.
    Rudement upgradesGrooveGROVOffShows and enables the Groove page in MIDI FX.
    Rudement upgradesReverb Filter HzRVHZOffShows the reverb HPF and LPF in Hz instead of 0–50. The sound and saved values are unchanged.
    Rudement upgradesGrid Follow LockLOCKOffEnables MIDI Follow: Grid Hold-to-Lock. Off is stock MIDI Follow.
    Top levelChord BrushBRSHOffEnables chord stamping in Chroma.
    Top levelKeyboard Note PreviewPREVOnLights sequenced notes on the keyboard grid during playback.
    Top levelRetrospective CaptureRCAPOffBuffers Keyboard View notes for SHIFT + RECORD capture.
    03How switches behave

    Most audio-feature switches control whether their menus are available. Settings already stored in a song remain saved. Delay Filters also bypasses its filtering when Off. Gesture features such as Kit Split, Scene Capture, Grid Column Reorder, Temp Hold, Harmonize, Strum, Loop Remix, Groove, Grid Follow Lock, Chord Brush, and Retrospective Capture do nothing until enabled.

    Safe starting point

    Leave the defaults as shown above. Enable the Off-by-default gestures when you intend to use them, and leave Delay Filters Off when you want the ordinary delay feedback path.

    A few four-letter codes are used twice on a 7-segment display: CHRD is both the Harmonize switch and the Bouls Chords model, and STRM is both the Strum switch and the Bouls String Machine model. The menu you are in tells you which one you are looking at.

    02Bouls
    Synthstrom Deluge · Rudement Firmware
    Chapter 02

    Bouls

    Operating manual for the 24-model oscillator engine

    Built from Mutable Instruments Plaits, Bouls brings its 24-model oscillator engine to the Deluge as an oscillator type. Twenty-four synthesis models share one front panel — Harmonics, Timbre and Morph — plus a low-pass gate and a choice of which of the engine's two outputs to use. The controls keep the same names in every model while their functions change from model to model; section 07 explains them model by model.

    Model · Harmonics · Timbre · Morph · LPG
    01What it is

    Bouls is available as an oscillator type: select it, and the sound uses whichever of its 24 synthesis models is dialled in instead of a conventional waveform. It is available on oscillator 1 only, and not in kits — the same restriction the DX7 engine has.

    Harmonics, Timbre and Morph are not new parameters bolted on beside the existing oscillator controls — they reuse three slots that already existed for other oscillator types (pulse-width, wave index, and a second pulse-width), running at the model's own front-panel meaning instead. That means all three patch, modulate and automate exactly the way pulse-width already did for a square wave, with no new patching surface to learn.

    Three things decide what you hear: which model is selected, where the three controls sit within that model, and whether the low-pass gate is in circuit. The third is the one people miss. With the LPG off, Bouls is a bare oscillator and the Deluge's own envelopes and filter do all the shaping; with it on, the engine gets the struck, blooming, vactrol-flavoured envelope that most of the module's recognisable sounds are made of. Section 04 covers what turning it on changes — which is more than an envelope, on four of the models.

    02Finding it

    Your first minute

    #Do thisAnd watch
    1Set oscillator 1's type to BOULS, then press SELECT on it againThe Bouls menu: model, three controls, the gate, and the aux output
    2Check Harmonics, Timbre and Morph are at 25A fresh Bouls sound starts all three at 25, the middle of every model's range, like a module with its knobs at noon. A sound that already had settings keeps them
    3Leave the model on Virtual Analog, set Morph to 50 and sweep TimbreThe plainest voice in the list. With Morph at 50 the saw drops out, so you hear Timbre alone: a thin pulse, a full square at 25, then hard sync past the middle
    4Turn Low-pass gate onThe same oscillator becomes a struck, blooming thing. This is the setting most of the recognisable sounds are made of
    5Change the model to Bass Drum, play an octave or two below middle C, and sweep MorphMorph is the decay on the drums: a tight tick at 0, a long boom at 50. Play softly and then hard: velocity sets the accent

    Select BOULS as the oscillator type, then press SELECT on it again to enter the Bouls menu: Bouls model, Harmonics, Timbre, Morph, Low-pass gate, LPG decay, LPG colour, and Aux output (which of the engine's two outputs you take). None of the toggles cut a held note when changed — the voice re-reads model, LPG and aux output every render block, so switching any of them mid-note swaps live rather than retriggering. The module itself isn't click-free when you do this either, so a small seam on model changes is expected, not a fault.

    The three continuous controls in this menu are the same parameters as Osc 1's Pulse Width and Wave Index and Osc 2's Pulse Width — a second door onto one room, not a copy. Editing them here, on the oscillator menus, from the shortcut grid, over MIDI or from automation are all the same edit.

    03Harmonics, Timbre and Morph

    Three controls, twenty-four meanings each. The menu never renames them per model — it says Harmonics, Timbre and Morph whichever model is loaded — so section 07 is the translation table, and it is the part of this chapter worth keeping open.

    Loosely, and with plenty of exceptions: Harmonics chooses what — the chord, the terrain, the patch, the filter mode, the spectrum's shape. Timbre is usually the brightness or density control, the one that behaves most like opening a filter. Morph is usually the waveform or the decay — the shape of the thing rather than its content. Learning a model means learning which of those three the model bent furthest.

    Travel, and where the useful part of it is

    ControlBorrowed slotMenu defaultWorking travel
    HarmonicsOsc 1 Pulse Width250 → 50 covers the model's full range
    TimbreOsc 1 Wave Index250 → 50 covers the model's full range
    MorphOsc 2 Pulse Width250 → 50 covers the model's full range

    All three run 0 to 50 across the engine's full range, and a fresh Bouls sound starts all three at 25, the middle of every model's range, where a module with its knobs at noon would be. Switching an oscillator to Bouls sets Harmonics and Morph to 25 only if they are still at the Deluge's untouched default and not automated, so a sound you have already shaped keeps its settings.

    Modulation adds to wherever the control is set. Harmonics and Morph stop at their ends; Timbre is centred, so a patch cable, LFO or envelope can push it both down and up from 25.

    Over MIDI and automation

    The three controls answer MIDI Follow on the Deluge's standard CCs for the slots they borrow: Harmonics CC 23, Timbre CC 25, Morph CC 28. All three cover the full 0–50 range from a controller, the Automation View lane and the gold knob, exactly as they do from the menu. If a controller knob seems to do nothing, check it is sending the right CC: the OLED names the parameter each incoming CC moves.

    Known limitations

    Morph borrows Oscillator 2's pulse width. If oscillator 2 is set to a square or pulse wave, its width and Bouls' Morph are the same control and cannot be set independently, and switching to Bouls leaves Morph where it is rather than moving oscillator 2's width to 25. Harmonics and Timbre are safe — they sit on oscillator 1's slots, which Bouls has taken over anyway.

    Model, Low-pass gate, LPG decay, LPG colour and Aux output are per-source settings rather than parameters: they are saved with the sound, but they cannot be automated, patched or MIDI-learned.

    04The low-pass gate, and what turning it on changes

    On the module the LPG is in circuit unless you patch the level input, and it supplies most of what people recognise as "Plaits" — the pluck, the bloom, the way a bright attack darkens as it falls away. Here it is a toggle, off by default, because a Deluge oscillator is expected to be a bare oscillator until told otherwise.

    Low-pass gate default off

    Off: the engine's raw output, no gate and no decay. The Deluge's own envelopes, filter and amplitude do all the work, and Bouls behaves like any other oscillator type.

    On: the gate is struck on each note-on and decays under LPG decay and LPG colour. Its attack scales with pitch, so low notes bloom noticeably more slowly than high ones. This is the setting for plucks, bongos, blooming pads and anything that should have a shape of its own before the Deluge's envelope touches it — and it stacks with that envelope rather than replacing it, so a slow Deluge attack over a struck LPG gives you both.

    LPG decay default 25

    The gate's decay time, from a click of a few milliseconds at 0 to a tail of well over a second at 50. It has no effect while the low-pass gate is off, and none on the eight self-enveloped models below.

    LPG colour default 25

    What kind of gate it is. At 0 it is a filter: the sound darkens as it decays, the vactrol behaviour. At 50 it is a plain amplitude gate — the tone holds and only the level falls. It also lengthens the tail slightly as it rises. Only read while the low-pass gate is on.

    The eight models that bring their own envelope

    These eight models provide their own amplitude shaping, so Low-pass gate, LPG decay, and LPG colour are inactive. Their decay comes from Morph or from the loaded FM patch.

    On these eight, velocity sets the accent, the job the LEVEL input does on the module: harder notes strike the drums with more punch, pluck the string and strike the resonator harder, and play the FM patches at a higher velocity. A velocity of about 100 matches the module with nothing patched. The Deluge's own velocity-to-level still applies on top, as on any other oscillator.

    The side effect: four models change behaviour, not just shape

    Turning the LPG on also hands the engine a trigger, and a handful of models read a trigger as a mode switch rather than as an envelope. On these, the LPG toggle is doing something bigger than adding a decay:

    • Chiptune — stops playing a chord and becomes an arpeggiator, advancing one step per note-on, with Timbre selecting the pattern instead of the inversion. The gate itself is bypassed, so you get the mode change without the decay.
    • Granular Cloud — the swarm stops free-running and fires a fresh burst of grains at each note-on.
    • Filtered Noise — the noise clock's range extends two octaves lower, and the clock resets at each note-on rather than drifting.
    • Speech — in the word banks, each note-on replays a whole word instead of the word being scrubbed by hand with Morph.

    Particle Noise and Filtered Noise also reseed their randomness on each note-on once the trigger is live, which makes repeated notes noticeably more consistent than they are with the LPG off.

    05The aux output

    Every model renders two signals at once. The main output is the model's headline sound; the aux output is a companion the same engine produced along the way — a second oscillator, the exciter before a resonator, a sub, a bit-crushed copy, or the other side of a stereo pair. Aux output chooses which of the two the voice takes.

    Both are computed either way, so the toggle costs nothing and can be flipped on a held note. It is not a mix and there is no blend control: you get one or the other. To hear both at once you need two tracks, since Bouls is oscillator 1 only.

    What aux gives you is listed per model in section 07, and gathered in the table in section 08. Two notes worth having up front: on the three 6-op FM banks the aux output is identical to the main one, so the toggle does nothing there; and levels differ markedly between the two outputs on some models, so expect to re-balance the track's volume after switching.

    06The 24 models

    The model list uses fixed indices 0–23 so saved sounds always reopen with the same engine. The menu shows the names, not the numbers; the numbers here are the list order. Virtual Analog, ninth in the list, is the default.

    07The models, one by one

    Each entry describes the voice, then what the three controls do to it, then what the aux output gives you instead. Where a control behaves differently either side of its centre, that is said — several of them are bipolar in effect even though the menu reads 0–50.

    00 · Virtual Analog VCF VAVC

    A saw-or-pulse oscillator and a sub-oscillator through a resonant low-pass filter with soft clipping at every stage. The only model with a filter of its own, and the one that can sound like a finished patch before the Deluge's filter touches it — a mono synth in a single oscillator slot.

    • Harmonics resonance, and the filter's slope. The centre is clean; resonance climbs toward both ends and screams at either extreme. The lower half runs both filter stages for a steeper, more polite four-pole; the upper half fades the second stage out for a rawer two-pole with more drive.
    • Timbre cutoff, ten octaves of it, tracking the note.
    • Morph the waveform: saw at the bottom, through square, to a narrow pulse at the top — with a sub-oscillator fading in at both extremes and absent in the middle.
    • Aux the filter's high-pass output instead of its low-pass: thin, buzzy, and useful under something else.
    01 · Phase Distortion PHDS

    Casio CZ-style phase distortion: a sine wave read through a warped phase, which produces filter-like sweeps and hollow resonant vowels with no filter anywhere in the signal path.

    • Harmonics the ratio between the carrier and the modulator that warps it, quantised to musical intervals rather than swept continuously.
    • Timbre how much distortion. At zero this model is a plain sine.
    • Morph the asymmetry of the warp — the pulse width of the distortion, from symmetrical to sharply skewed.
    • Aux the same shaping free-running instead of hard-synced: phase modulation rather than phase distortion, less vocal and more bell-like.
    02–04 · 6-op FM A, B and C FMAFMBFMC

    Three banks of thirty-two six-operator FM patches — the DX7 architecture, complete with each patch's own operator envelopes and LFO. The three banks are three different sets of thirty-two, selected as three separate models rather than by a bank control.

    • Harmonics patch select within the bank: thirty-two of them, stepped with hysteresis so a wobbling modulator does not flicker between neighbours.
    • Timbre brightness — it scales the operators' output levels, which is FM's equivalent of opening a filter.
    • Morph envelope control. At 0 the patch's own envelopes run at their snappiest — short and percussive; raising it stretches them out toward their full length.
    • Aux identical to the main output. The toggle does nothing on these three.

    Self-enveloped: the LPG toggle, decay and colour are all inert; the patch's envelopes follow the note instead. Velocity reaches the patch as DX7 velocity. Two voices are rendered round-robin inside the engine, so a fast retrigger does not cut the previous note's tail. The banks are the factory ones — the module's ability to load your own SysEx bank from a card is not wired up here.

    05 · Wave Terrain TERR

    An orbit traced across a three-dimensional landscape, where the height under the pointer is the waveform. Tight orbits stay near a sine; wide ones cross ridges and gullies and turn spiky and complex.

    • Harmonics which terrain — eight of them, crossfaded rather than switched.
    • Timbre the radius of the orbit: how much of the terrain the trace covers, and so how far from a sine it gets. It is automatically reined in on high notes.
    • Morph the orbit's offset across the terrain — where the loop sits, and how lopsided it becomes.
    • Aux a sine reading of the orbit summed with the terrain height: a softer, more harmonic relative of the same motion.
    06 · String Machine STRM

    Four divide-down organ voices playing a chord, through a low-pass filter and an ensemble chorus. A Solina in a box, and the most immediately usable pad in the list.

    • Harmonics the chord, from the eleven-chord bank in section 08.
    • Timbre filter cutoff and the ensemble together: brightness rises across the whole travel, while the chorus is at its strongest at both ends and falls to nothing in the middle.
    • Morph the registration — drawbars, in effect. Square at the bottom, through saw and stacked saws, to a bright full registration with upper harmonics at the top.
    • Aux the other side of the ensemble's stereo pair: the same chord, different chorus phase.
    07 · Chiptune CHIP

    Four square-wave voices and a bass note, deliberately crude: a 1980s console sound chip, phase-inverted voice by voice so the chord fizzes the way those chips did.

    • Harmonics the chord.
    • Timbre the inversion — which note of the chord sits on top. With the LPG on, it selects the arpeggiator pattern instead.
    • Morph pulse width, from a full square to a thin, nasal buzz.
    • Aux the bass square alone, an octave below the root.

    With the low-pass gate on, this model becomes an arpeggiator: one note per note-on, stepping through the chord, with the gate itself bypassed. That is a mode change rather than an envelope — see section 04.

    18 · Virtual Analog VANAdefault model

    Two oscillators — a variable-width square and a variable-shape saw — mixed together. The plainest and most predictable voice in the list, and the right one for learning what the three controls feel like.

    • Harmonics detuning between the two oscillators, from unison to a wide beat.
    • Timbre the square: its level fades up from silence at the very bottom, then its pulse width narrows, and past the middle it hard-syncs, sweeping the classic sync tear.
    • Morph the saw: shape and width, with its level falling away as the control rises, so the top of the travel is square-dominant and the bottom is saw-dominant.
    • Aux "monster sync" — both oscillators self-synced under Timbre, harsher and more metallic than the main mix.
    08 · Waveshaping WSHP

    A band-limited slope through a waveshaper and then a wavefolder — the West Coast timbre, where a control that looks like a level control turns into a brightness control.

    • Harmonics which waveshaping curve, interpolated across a table. The centre is neutral; both directions bend the curve further, and the range is automatically narrowed on high notes to keep the folding from aliasing.
    • Timbre wavefolder drive: how many folds, and so how many overtones. At 0 there is no folding at all and the model sounds nearly inert — this is the model most often written off from its default.
    • Morph the slope's shape and pulse width: the asymmetry going into the shaper.
    • Aux a sine crossfaded with a second fold curve — the same gesture with the top taken off, and a good deal easier on the ears.
    16 · 2-op FM FM2

    One sine modulating another, plus a sub-oscillator — the two-operator FM from Braids, Rings and Elements. Bells, basses, clangs and electric pianos.

    • Harmonics the modulator's frequency ratio, quantised to a table of musical ratios, so it lands on intervals rather than sliding between them.
    • Timbre the FM index — the amount of modulation, and therefore the brightness. It is automatically tamed on high notes to hold aliasing down.
    • Morph feedback, bipolar: the centre is clean, below it the feedback goes to the carrier's phase, above it to the modulator's. The two directions sound quite different — one grows a rasp, the other a growl.
    • Aux the sub-oscillator, an octave down and itself modulated by the carrier: a fatter, darker version of the same event.
    09 · Granular Formant FORM

    Two grain oscillators whose windows produce a formant peak — a vowel-like, VOSIM-flavoured sound that is pitched by the note and coloured by where the formant sits.

    • Harmonics the ratio between the two formants, spread over four octaves; below the centre it also bleeds the raw carrier back in, which thickens the low end.
    • Timbre the formant frequency itself — the vowel, in effect, sweeping seven octaves.
    • Morph the shape of the grain window, from soft to sharply pinched.
    • Aux a different formant oscillator at the same pitch: one cleaner peak instead of two interfering ones.
    10 · Harmonic HARM

    Additive synthesis: twenty-four harmonics whose amplitudes are drawn by three controls rather than twenty-four faders. Organs, bells, and spectra that no filter would produce.

    • Harmonics the number of peaks in the spectrum, from a single broad bump up to sixteen — one peak is a formant, many is a comb.
    • Timbre where the peak sits: which harmonic is loudest. Sweeping it is the closest thing here to a band-pass sweep.
    • Morph the slope — how sharply the amplitudes fall away from the peak. Shallow slopes are bright and buzzy, steep ones nearly sinusoidal.
    • Aux eight organ harmonics — octaves and fifths only — instead of the full integer series: a drawbar organ standing next to a spectrum.
    11 · Wavetable WTBL

    A grid of waves read as a smooth surface, with two axes of position and a third of bank. Sweeping any of the three is the sound of this model.

    • Harmonics the bank. Past the middle of its travel the interpolation between waves is progressively quantised, and the model turns deliberately steppy and lo-fi — that crunch is the design, not a fault.
    • Timbre position along a row: eight waves, crossfaded.
    • Morph position down the column: eight rows, crossfaded.
    • Aux the same wave crushed to five bits — a dirtier twin of whatever the main output is doing.
    12 · Chords CHRD

    Four notes from a bank of eleven chords, played by divide-down organ voices that hand over one at a time to a wavetable of string and vocal waves at the top of Morph. One key, one chord, and a bass note on the aux output.

    • Harmonics the chord, stepped through the eleven-chord bank in section 08.
    • Timbre the inversion: it rotates the voicing upward one note at a time, crossfading rather than jumping, which makes it usable as a modulation destination.
    • Morph the tone. The bottom is the fullest, brightest organ registration, thinning through saws to a plain square by about the middle; past that the four notes cross one by one into the wavetable and the chord turns to strings and voices.
    • Aux the root note alone. This is how one voice gives you a bass line and a chord — on two tracks, or by switching.
    20 · Speech SPCH

    Three speech synthesisers stacked behind one control: a naive formant filter, a re-creation of SAM (the 1982 home-computer voice) and an LPC synthesiser with banks of stored words.

    • Harmonics which synthesiser, and what it can say. The first sixth of the travel crossfades the naive formant filter into SAM; the next sixth crossfades SAM into LPC vowels; the remaining two-thirds step through five banks of LPC words — numbers, letters and so on.
    • Timbre formant shift: the size of the speaker, from a giant down to a chipmunk, without changing pitch.
    • Morph the address — which phoneme, vowel or word. Sweeping it by hand is how you get the talking-through-a-scrubbed-tape effect.
    • Aux the excitation alone: the glottal buzz before the formants, which is a usable raw source in its own right.

    With the low-pass gate on, the word banks replay a whole word at each note-on instead of being scrubbed by Morph.

    13 · Granular Cloud CLUD

    A swarm of detuned voices doing random walks around the note — less a chord than a cloud, and the model that best rewards a slow modulation on all three controls at once.

    • Harmonics the spread: how far the swarm wanders from the root, from a tight unison shimmer to a smear across octaves.
    • Timbre the density and rate of the swarm's motion.
    • Morph grain duration — long grains hold pitch, short ones turn the cloud into texture.
    • Aux the same swarm rendered as sines rather than saws: softer, more choral, far less harsh at high densities.

    With the low-pass gate on it switches to burst mode: each note-on fires a fresh burst of grains rather than running continuously.

    15 · Filtered Noise NOIS

    Clocked noise through a resonant multimode filter. It covers everything from wind and surf to a pitched whistle, and it is the model to reach for when a track needs air rather than notes.

    • Harmonics two things at once: the filter mode, sweeping continuously from low-pass through band-pass to high-pass, and the pitch offset of the second band-pass that appears on the aux output.
    • Timbre the noise clock. At the bottom the noise is slow, stepped and gritty; at the top it is full-band hiss.
    • Morph resonance, from a broad wash up to a self-oscillating whistle at the note's pitch.
    • Aux two band-pass filters summed instead of the single multimode filter: a two-peaked, more vocal noise.

    With the low-pass gate on, the noise clock's range extends two octaves lower and resets at each note-on.

    17 · Particle Noise PART

    Random pulses fired through randomly-tuned band-pass filters: rain, crackle, Geiger counters, and — at high density with resonance up — something close to a struck metal sheet.

    • Harmonics how widely the filter frequencies scatter around the note, from all-in-tune to four octaves of confetti.
    • Timbre density: how often a particle fires, from occasional ticks to a continuous rustle.
    • Morph split at its centre. Below it, a diffuser smears the particles into a cloud, most heavily at the bottom; above it the band-passes get resonant and each particle rings instead of clicking.
    • Aux the raw pulses before any filtering: bare clicks rather than pings.
    14 · Inharmonic String STRG

    A plucked string model with a stiffness term, so it runs from nylon through piano wire to things that stopped being strings some way back.

    • Harmonics inharmonicity. There is a deliberate dead zone right at the centre where the string is clean and harmonic; move either way and it grows progressively more dispersed and bell-like, with the two directions taking different routes there.
    • Timbre the brightness of the pluck — the filter on the excitation burst, from a soft thumb to a hard plectrum.
    • Morph damping: how long the string rings after the pluck.
    • Aux the raw excitation burst without the string — a short filtered noise click.

    Self-enveloped: the LPG toggle and its decay and colour are inert, and Morph is the decay control. The string is always plucked here — the module's continuously-excited, bowed behaviour needs a level input the Deluge does not provide.

    19 · Modal Resonator MODL

    A bank of tuned modes struck by an impulse: bells, bars, bowls, tubes and gongs. The same family as the string above, with the resonator's tuning opened up instead of its stiffness.

    • Harmonics the inharmonicity of the mode series — harmonic and string-like at one end, sharply metallic at the other. It is deliberately smoothed, so sweeping it glides rather than steps.
    • Timbre the brightness of the strike: how much energy goes into the upper modes.
    • Morph damping — a dead thud at the bottom, a long ring at the top.
    • Aux the exciter alone, without the resonator.

    Self-enveloped, exactly as the string: LPG inert, Morph is the decay, always struck rather than continuously excited.

    21 · Bass Drum BASS

    Two bass drums rendered at once: an 808-style bridged-T circuit on the main output, and a synthetic, FM-flavoured drum on the aux.

    • Harmonics the punch, in three stages as it climbs: attack FM first, then self-FM, then overdrive. From about 13 upward the self-FM bends the pitch up while the drum is loud, and a longer Morph keeps it loud for longer, so the pitch rise grows with the decay. Keep Harmonics at about 10 or below for a drum that holds its pitch.
    • Timbre tone — the balance of click and body.
    • Morph decay, from a tight tick to a long boom.
    • Aux the synthetic drum instead of the analogue one: tighter, more modern, more distorted.

    Self-enveloped. LPG decay does nothing here — Morph is the decay control. The drum is tuned to the note you play, so middle C gives a 130 Hz drum; play an octave or two lower for a kick.

    22 · Snare Drum SNAR

    An 808-style analogue snare — two tuned resonators and a noise burst — on the main output, with a synthetic snare on the aux.

    • Harmonics snappy: the balance between the drum's tone and the snare rattle.
    • Timbre tone — the pitch balance and brightness of the two resonators.
    • Morph decay.
    • Aux the synthetic snare: harder, more processed, with more FM in the body.

    Self-enveloped, same as the bass drum: Morph is the decay, and the LPG controls do nothing.

    23 · Hi-Hat HHAT

    Six square oscillators at inharmonic ratios plus noise, filtered and gated — the 808 recipe on the main output, with a more metallic alternative on the aux.

    • Harmonics noisiness: the balance between the square cluster and plain noise.
    • Timbre tone — the filtering, from dark and closed to bright and open.
    • Morph decay, which is what makes this the same model for both a closed and an open hat.
    • Aux the metallic variant: a different noise source, harder and more ringing.

    Self-enveloped: Morph is the decay, the LPG controls are inert.

    The three controls, twenty-four ways

    The chord bank

    Harmonics steps through the same eleven chords in Chords, String Machine and Chiptune, in this order:

    #Chord#Chord#Chord
    1Octave5Minor 7th9Major 9th
    2Fifth6Minor 9th10Major 7th
    3Sus47Minor 11th11Major
    4Minor86/9

    The order runs from the emptiest intervals up through the minor family to the major one, so sweeping Harmonics walks the harmony rather than jumping around it. Steps are quantised with hysteresis, so a modulated Harmonics settles on a chord instead of chattering between two.

    03Four-Band EQ
    Synthstrom Deluge · Rudement Firmware
    Chapter 03

    Four-Band EQ

    Operating manual for the two added mid bells

    The EQ has four bands: a bass shelf, two bell bands named Low mid and High mid, and a treble shelf. Amount controls display dB and frequency controls display Hz instead of a bare 0–50 value.

    Bass · Low mid · High mid · Treble
    01What it is

    Two bell bands, added between the existing bass and treble shelves. They are not built the way a parametric EQ's bell usually is — there is no biquad peaking filter here. Each band is the difference of two one-pole lowpasses, a low corner subtracted from a high corner, which peaks at the geometric mean of the two and falls away on both sides. It behaves like a bell on the knob; structurally it is a subtraction.

    That construction has one consequence worth knowing before you judge the range: a band built this way never passes the full extracted signal at its peak. The low mid captures about 64% of what it pulls out at its neutral centre, the high mid about 60%. Both mid bands are therefore mixed in at ×6 rather than the ×4 the shelves use, which is what gets them to the same useful ±12 dB or so range from a smaller starting capture.

    02Finding it

    Your first minute

    #Do thisAnd watch
    1Put a bright loop on a track and open FX → EQEight controls, four bands. Every one reads in real dB or Hz, not 0–50
    2Take Low mid amount to the bottomThe popup reads OFF rather than a number — the band has cancelled, and a floor is more honest than a rising negative
    3Bring it back to 250.0 dB. Centre is the detent on all eight controls
    4Sweep Low mid freq up past knob 41The readout stops moving. The upper pole has pinned — that is the band's range, not a stuck encoder
    5Now cut instead of boostingA cut goes markedly deeper than a boost reaches. That asymmetry is the amount law, and it is the fastest way to hear where a band actually sits

    The EQ occupies the same slot stock Deluge EQ always has, late in the global FX chain.

    All four EQ bands occupy the same late position in the global effects chain.

    03The controls

    Menu position 25 is centre / the detent on every one of these eight controls. The figures show the values reported by the controls.

    Bass & Treble (the shelves)

    KnobBass cornerTreble corner
    0~3 Hz~36 Hz
    25 (centre)~199 Hz~2.77 kHz
    32~658 Hz20 kHz (ceiling)
    5020 kHz (ceiling)20 kHz (ceiling)

    Both shelves sweep ±6 octaves around their centre corner. Amount reaches exactly ±12 dB at the ends of its knob and is flat (0 dB) at centre. Treble's Freq knob reaches the display ceiling of 20 kHz by knob position 32, and from there up the Treble amount knob does nothing at all, because there is nothing left above that frequency for the shelf to act on.

    Low mid & High mid (the bells)

    Knob (Freq)Low mid centreHigh mid centre
    0~120 Hz~910 Hz
    25 (centre)~1.04 kHz~2.0 kHz
    41~6.4 kHz (upper pole pinning)—
    50pinned near 10–20 kHz~5.6 kHz
    Knob (Amount)Low mid gainHigh mid gain
    0OFF*−20.0 dB
    12−11.5 dB−10.2 dB
    25 (centre)0.0 dB0.0 dB
    38+7.0 dB+6.8 dB
    50+11.7 dB+11.4 dB

    * Below −24 dB the popup reads OFF rather than a number — the bells actually cancel a hair past zero at the bottom of their travel, and a display floor is more honest than a negative-then-rising number as you wind the knob back up.

    Known limitations

    Low mid's upper pole pins from around Freq knob 41 — above that, moving the knob further doesn't move the band, it's already sitting at the display ceiling.

    Treble's amount does nothing above Freq knob 32, for the same reason: there is nothing left above it to shelve.

    04The curve, and its eight markers

    On an OLED the EQ menu draws the whole response as one line, with a small square sitting on it for every control. There are eight squares, one per control, and the selected one is filled rather than hollow — so the square that inverts as you turn the select encoder tells you which control you are about to change.

    How the eight markers are arranged

    Every band has an Amount control and a Frequency control, so every band contributes two squares.

    The shelf markers occupy the outer ends of the response: Amount rides the flat plateau and Frequency marks the corner where that plateau joins the centre line. Bass is on the left and Treble mirrors it on the right.

    The two bell bands occupy separate regions between the shelf corners. Low mid uses the left half and High mid uses the right half. Each Frequency square marks the band's horizontal position; its Amount square marks the height of the bell.

    At a neutral mid Amount there is no raised or lowered bell, so its Amount square would normally land on its Frequency square. The OLED separates the Amount square slightly along the same flat response line, keeping all eight controls visible. As soon as the Amount leaves centre, that square moves to the bell's peak while the Frequency square remains on the centre line.

    05Displays and defaults
    Control7SEGDefault
    Bass amount / freqBASS / BAFRcentre (0 dB) / ~199 Hz
    Treble amount / freqTREB / TRFRcentre (0 dB) / ~2.77 kHz
    Low mid amount / freqLMID / LMFRcentre (0 dB) / ~1.04 kHz
    High mid amount / freqHMID / HMFRcentre (0 dB) / ~2.0 kHz
    Switching it off entirely

    SETTINGS → COMMUNITY FEATURES → Rudement upgrades → Four-Band EQ (EQ4), on by default. Switching it off hides only the two mid bands. Bass and treble are stock Deluge and stay exactly where they are, dB/Hz readouts included — this toggle does not touch them.

    04Delay & Reverb Filters
    Synthstrom Deluge · Rudement Firmware
    Chapter 04

    Delay & Reverb Filters

    Shape delay repeats and the shared wet reverb return

    Two pairs of filters solve different problems: delay filters work inside each feedback loop, while reverb filters shape the song's shared wet return.

    DLYF · FX → DELAY · FX → REVERB · HPF · LPF

    Your first minute

    #Do thisAnd watch
    1Turn on SETTINGS → COMMUNITY FEATURES → Rudement upgrades → Delay FiltersOff by default. HPF and LPF appear in FX → DELAY
    2Put a short, bright sound on a track, open FX → DELAY and give it some feedbackOrdinary repeats, each a copy of the last
    3Raise HPFEach repeat is thinner than the one before. The dry sound does not change
    4Lower LPFEach repeat is darker. The display shows the cutoff in Hz
    5Open FX → REVERB and lower its LPFThe shared reverb tail darkens for every track at once. No switch needed
    01Delay feedback filters

    Delay Filters places a high-pass filter and a low-pass filter inside the delay feedback path. The dry signal is unchanged. Each repeat passes through the filters again, so echoes can become progressively thinner, darker, or both.

    02Finding the delay filters

    Enable SETTINGS → COMMUNITY FEATURES → Rudement upgrades → Delay Filters, then open FX → DELAY. On a Kit, use Affect Entire when you want the setting applied across the kit.

    03Delay controls
    ControlRangeBypass positionApproximate sweep
    HPF0–500About 20 Hz at 1 to about 1 kHz at 50
    LPF0–5050About 300 Hz at 0 to about 16 kHz at 49

    The display reports the calculated cutoff in hertz. Use HPF to reduce low-frequency buildup and LPF to restrict the upper range of the repeats. These are saved settings rather than automation parameters and have no default CC.

    04Delay bypass and saved values

    Turning the Delay Filters Community Features switch Off hides both delay controls and bypasses both delay filters. Their cutoff values remain saved and return when the switch is turned On again.

    05Reverb filters

    The Reverb HPF and LPF shape the shared wet return without altering dry tracks. The Mutable and Digital models carry these filters from the stock firmware; Rudement adds the same HPF and LPF to Freeverb, which had none — so all three models now share one filtered return. Every track send feeds it.

    06Finding the reverb filters

    Open FX → REVERB, choose any reverb Model, then open HPF or LPF. These song-level controls are saved with the song. They read 0–50, as on stock firmware; turn on SETTINGS → COMMUNITY FEATURES → Rudement upgrades → Reverb Filter Hz (RVHZ) to read them in Hz instead.

    07Reverb controls
    ControlRangeDefaultApproximate cutoffUse
    HPF0–50020 Hz / 300 Hz / 890 Hz at 0 / 25 / 50Raise it to remove bass and low-mid buildup from the wet tail.
    LPF0–5050Closed / 5.68 kHz / 17.7 kHz at 0 / 25 / 50Lower it to darken the wet tail; 0 closes the wet return.

    The controls filter the wet return only. HPF at 0 is a protective 20 Hz low cut. LPF at 50 is the most open setting. With Reverb Filter Hz On, HPF reads 20Hz to 890Hz and LPF reads CLOSED at 0, then up to 17.7kHz at 50.

    08Reverb damping is different

    Damping darkens later reflections as the tail recirculates; LPF filters the completed wet return. Both reverb filters change the one shared reverb for the entire song. Individual tracks still set their send level with Reverb Amount.

    Switching it off entirely

    SETTINGS → COMMUNITY FEATURES → Rudement upgrades → Delay Filters (DLYF), Off by default. Off hides both delay filter controls and bypasses the filters; their values are kept and come back when you turn it On. The reverb HPF and LPF are always there; SETTINGS → COMMUNITY FEATURES → Rudement upgrades → Reverb Filter Hz (RVHZ, Off by default) only changes how they read.

    05Sear
    Synthstrom Deluge · Rudement Firmware
    Chapter 05

    Sear

    Operating manual for the auto-levelling drive stage

    A cubic soft clipper with automatic level matching, followed by a one-pole tilt tone control. It is per voice and patchable, so it behaves like other modulation destinations.

    Sear · STon
    01What it is

    Sear is a cubic soft clipper. Compared with the stock Saturation stage it has a harder knee and a true ceiling, so it reads as "pedal" beside the softer stock drive. It is light enough to run on every voice.

    Aliasing

    There is no oversampling, and the cubic curve generates harmonics up to 3× the input frequency, so bright material driven hard will alias. Sear sits after the ladder filter in the signal path, so rolling the low-pass down also tames the aliasing — that's the practical fix, not a setting on the effect itself.

    02Finding it

    Your first minute

    #Do thisAnd watch
    1On a synth clip, open FX → DistortionSear and STon sit with the other per-voice distortion stages
    2Bring Sear up from the bottomAudible by knob 3–5. There is no dead zone; the taper is a constant ratio per step
    3Take it to 25, then 5016× pre-gain, then 256×. The output barely gets louder — the level matching is removing what the drive would otherwise add
    4Play softly, then hardYour dynamics survive. It tracks the ratio across the clipper, not a level, so it is not behaving like a compressor
    5Take STon either side of centreA tilt. Centre is a true bypass, measured flat, so the tone control changes nothing until you move it

    FX → Distortion, alongside the other per-voice distortion stages — Saturation, Bitcrush, Decimation and Wavefold — as Sear (the drive) and STon (its tone control). Because it is patched and per-voice, it appears on synth clips and drums, not on kit-global or song FX.

    03Sear (the drive)

    A patched param, so it can be modulated like any other. Pre-gain sweeps on an exponential taper — roughly a constant ratio per knob step, audible from knob position 3–5 with no dead zone:

    Knob035101520253035404550
    Gain1.0×1.5×1.8×3.2×5.6×9.6×16×29×51×90×154×256×
    Automatic level matching

    Two one-pole followers track mean absolute level either side of the clipper, over roughly a 23 ms window, and the correction applied is their ratio. This is not a compressor and does not behave like one — it tracks the ratio of two levels, not a level, so when the input gets quieter the output gets quieter with it and the ratio barely moves. Ordinary note dynamics pass through untouched; only the amount the clipper is adding is corrected. A small loudness lift is kept on purpose so the drive does not feel like nothing is happening: the output rises gently with the knob, about +2.3 dB at the top.

    New notes start from the sound's existing level estimate, so only the very first note a sound plays is measured from cold.

    04STon (the tone control)

    An unpatched tilt tone control shaping what the drive bites on. A one-pole split into low and high halves, weighted so that at centre both halves sum back to the input exactly — measured flat to 0.00 dB. The pivot sits near 1 kHz, where a guitar-pedal tone stack usually puts it.

    100 Hz1 kHz8 kHz
    Dark (min)+5.8 dB−1.7 dB−18.5 dB
    Centre (default)0.0 dB0.0 dB0.0 dB
    Bright (max)−7.6 dB+4.9 dB+5.7 dB
    05Controls, limits and feature switch
    Control7SEGDefault
    SearSEARminimum (bypass)
    STonSToncentre (flat)
    Known limitations

    Aliasing on bright or hard-driven material — see section 01. The remedy is to roll the filter down ahead of it.

    Switching it off entirely

    SETTINGS → COMMUNITY FEATURES → Rudement upgrades → Sear (SEAR), on by default. Hides the Sear drive and tone controls; processing already dialled in keeps running.

    06Gristleator
    Synthstrom Deluge · Rudement Firmware
    Chapter 06

    Gristleator

    Operating manual for the chop, throb, and tempo-locked Slicer

    A modulation and distortion effect with a free-running LFO, a tempo-locked sixteen-step Slicer, parallel amplitude and filter stages, and fourteen controls including a master On switch.

    On · Rate · Depth · Shape · Bias · Mode · Freq · Reso · Dirt · Level · Pattern · Variation · Sync · Blend
    01What it is

    The free-running LFO drives two parallel stages: an amplitude stage (the chop) and a state-variable filter (the throb), blended by Mode. The Slicer adds a song-synchronised sixteen-step pattern beside the LFO. Its first lane controls amplitude; its second lane controls the filter or, for Grind, Dirt.

    The Gristleator sits late in the global FX chain.

    02Finding it

    Your first minute

    #Do thisAnd watch
    1Open FX → GRISOn is the first item because it is the master bypass for the other thirteen controls
    2Switch On on, then take Depth to about 35Tremolo. Most of the audible change is in the bottom half of that knob
    3Take Shape to maximumThe triangle squares off and the chop reads as a hard gate rather than a swell
    4Push Mode fully overThe amplitude chop disappears and the LFO sweeps a resonant filter instead. Turning Depth down here does not bypass it — a static filter stays in the path
    5Take Rate to the very topThe LFO crosses into audio rate and the chop stops being tremolo and starts being a second tone
    6Set Blend to 50, Pattern to Interlock, and Sync to 1/16Volume lands on the beat while the filter moves offbeat. Move Mode toward the middle to hear both lanes

    Fourteen shared controls serve Synths, Kits with Affect Entire, Audio Clips, and Song FX. The menu paginates 4/4/4/2 across four pages. On remains first as the master bypass; Pattern, Variation, Sync, and Blend follow Level.

    03The master switch

    On is bipolar and thresholded at centre: values above centre are On, while centre and below are Off. Switching it crossfades between the untouched signal and the complete Gristleator so the transition remains smooth.

    04The controls

    In signal order: the driver, then what it drives, then the output stage.

    ControlDefaultWhat it does
    RatecentreLFO speed. Rates through the knob's whole travel, from a slow sweep up into audio rate — pushed far enough, the chop stops reading as tremolo and starts reading as a second tone.
    Depth0 (min)How far the LFO pulls the stage down. Zero is an exact bypass of the modulation — both stages still pass signal, just unmodulated. Warped so roughly −6 dB of chop already arrives by mid-travel; most of the audible change is in the bottom half of the knob, not the top.
    Shape0 (min)Triangle → trapezoid → square, continuously. Minimum is a plain triangle.
    BiascentreOffsets the LFO before shaping. Bipolar; pushed hard enough it rails the LFO fully open or fully shut — faithful to Carter's front-panel mod, not a bug.
    Mode0 (min — VCA)0 = pure VCA (chop), full = pure VCF (throb), continuously blendable in between.
    Freq ("Register")centre (~800 Hz)Filter centre. Bipolar, ±2 octaves, so the knob covers roughly 200 Hz to 3.2 kHz.
    Reso0 (min)Filter resonance. Stops short of self-oscillation by design — a saturating stage in the filter's feedback path bounds it, so the top of the knob is a resonant sweep, not a squeal.
    Dirt0 (min — clean)Blends the clean VCA output against a driven, soft-clipped one. Drive rises alongside the mix — up to 3× — so turning Dirt up both adds distortion and pushes it harder, the way a JFET stage in the original circuit distorts more as it's driven harder. Sits after the VCA, so it's the chop itself being distorted, not a static overdrive with a tremolo bolted on after it.
    Levelmax (unity)Output trim.
    PatternFourSelects one of twelve sixteen-step rhythms. The first eight use the same rhythm for both lanes; Interlock, Cross, Sweep, and Grind give the second lane a different rhythm.
    Variation0Selects one of eleven repeatable rearrangements of the current pattern. Variation 0 is the named base pattern.
    Sync1/16Sets each step to 1/32, 1/16T, 1/16, 1/8T, 1/8, 1/4, 1/2, or one bar.
    Blend0 (LFO)Minimum is the LFO alone, centre multiplies the LFO by the pattern, and maximum is the pattern alone.
    05The two-lane Slicer

    Each pattern has sixteen steps. Lane A controls the amplitude. Lane B normally controls the filter; Grind sends Lane B to Dirt instead. Depth sets how far the selected stages move, so Depth 0 produces no rhythmic modulation even when Blend is raised.

    PatternLane A · volumeLane B · filter or Dirt
    FourOn every beatSame rhythm
    EighthsEvery other stepSame rhythm
    OffbeatBetween the beatsSame rhythm
    GallopLong-short-shortSame rhythm
    BurstFour on, four offSame rhythm
    TripletThree against the barSame rhythm
    SyncopatedOffset accentsSame rhythm
    TremoloEvery step; Bias sets dutySame rhythm
    InterlockOn the beatFilter on the offbeat
    CrossEighthsFilter in a three-over-two feel
    SweepConstant; no volume chopFilter opens in bursts of four
    GrindEighthsDirt arrives on the beat; raise Dirt to hear it
    Mode and Lane B

    For Interlock, Cross, and Sweep, Mode determines how much of the amplitude lane and filter lane reaches the output. At Mode 0 only the VCA path is heard; at maximum only the filter path is heard. Grind places Lane B inside the VCA path at Dirt, so raise Dirt and keep Mode below maximum to hear its second rhythm.

    06Shape, Bias, Blend, and timing

    Shape and Bias also shape the Slicer. Shape controls the attack and release speed of each step; Bias controls how long each step stays open. Lane B uses slower edges than Lane A so filter movement remains smooth.

    Blend positionWhat drives the effect
    0Free-running LFO only
    25LFO multiplied by the tempo-locked pattern
    50Tempo-locked pattern only

    The pattern cycle follows the song position. Starting playback begins on the downbeat, and stopping and restarting returns it there. Pattern and Variation changes take effect at the next step. Sync changes wait for a closed Lane A gate, stopped transport, or the next beat to keep the timing change smooth.

    Operating limits

    The Slicer changes level, filter, and Dirt; it does not pitch-shift slices. With Blend at 0, only the free-running LFO is active. With Blend above 0, both pattern lanes run regardless of the Mode setting.

    07Starting points

    Five settings worth dialling in as-is, then pulling apart. Knob values are approximate on-screen positions on a bipolar 0–50 scale (25 = centre).

    Classic chop On · Mode 0 · Shape 0 · Rate 30 · Depth 35 · Level 50

    Steady tremolo — a plain triangle LFO chopping the amplitude at a moderate rate.

    Square gate On · Mode 0 · Shape 50 · Depth 50 · Rate 28

    Shape at maximum turns the LFO into a near-square wave, so the chop reads as a hard gate rather than a swell.

    Throb filter sweep On · Mode 50 · Freq 30 · Reso 35 · Depth 30

    Mode fully toward the filter removes the amplitude chop entirely — the LFO sweeps a resonant filter instead, with no gating.

    Dirty chop On · Mode 0 · Dirt 35 · Depth 30

    The chop itself gets driven harder as it opens, rather than a clean chop followed by static distortion.

    Audio-rate buzz On · Mode 0 · Depth 40 · Rate 48–50

    Push Rate to the very top of its travel and the LFO crosses into audio-rate territory — the chop stops sounding like tremolo and starts sounding like a second, ring-mod-like tone.

    07Wisps
    Synthstrom Deluge · Rudement Firmware
    Chapter 07

    Wisps

    Operating manual for the six-mode texture engine

    Built from Mutable Instruments Clouds, Wisps brings its six-mode texture engine to the Deluge as an instrument effect: on a synth, on a single kit row, or on an Audio Clip — one instance at a time. Six processing modes share one front panel — Mode, Blend, Position, Size, Pitch, Density, Texture, Spread, Feedback, Reverb and Freeze. The controls keep the same names in every mode while their functions change from mode to mode; section 03 explains them mode by mode. Blend at 0 is an exact dry bypass.

    Mode · Blend · Position · Size · Pitch · Density · Texture · Spread · Feedback · Reverb · Freeze
    01What it is

    One recording buffer, about a second of audio, and six different ways of reading back out of it. Wisps is a texture generator rather than a colouring effect — it does not add an identifiable character to a signal so much as take it apart and rebuild it.

    Six modes share eleven controls, and several controls have a different meaning in each mode. Use the per-mode table in section 03 as the reference.

    Where it sits in the chain

    Wisps runs at the head of the track's FX chain — after the source (a synth's or kit row's voices and Sear, or an Audio Clip's render, saturation and filters) and the SRR/bitcrush distortion, but ahead of ModFX, the Gristleator, EQ, delay and the reverb send. It sits in the same place on all three. Putting it first means it works on the raw signal, and the rest of the chain then shapes the result.

    02Finding it

    Your first minute

    #Do thisAnd watch
    1On a synth, open FX → DUST and set Mode to GranularNothing yet. The engine allocates its buffer, but Blend starts fully dry on purpose
    2Bring Blend up to about 30Grains. This is the sound Wisps is known for
    3Take Density down to 28Silence. That is Granular's silent band; the default of 40 stays clear of it
    4Put Density back and switch Freeze onThe buffer stops taking new audio and becomes an instrument. Sweep Position through what you captured
    5Change Mode to OliverbThe old mode fades out, the new one fades in — a short dip, no click. Blend stays where you left it

    Wisps is an instrument effect. It lives on the FX submenu of a synth, a kit row or an Audio Clip, and its 7-segment name is DUST.

    ContextPath
    Synth clipFX → DUST
    A single kit rowFX → DUST
    Audio ClipFX → DUST
    Song FX, or a kit's Affect Entire FXnot available — one engine on the master bus starved everything else
    One at a time

    The Deluge can run one Wisps. On the unit even two Granulars together overload it — each is cheap alone, but two engines fight over the same memory. So while one Wisps is running, picking a mode anywhere else is refused with "Wisps is already turned on elsewhere. Turn that one off first" and that menu stays on OFF. To move Wisps, switch the first one OFF, then turn it on where you want it — or resample the first track and free it up.

    A Wisps that has been silent for about a second — Blend at 0 on a track that is not playing — does not count, so a forgotten one can never lock you out. If two do end up running at once (a song saved that way, or a synth duplicated with Wisps on), the overload guard steps in: once the CPU stays overloaded, the more recently switched-on one fades out, switches itself OFF, and "CPU overloaded: newest Wisps switched off" appears.

    Automation, MIDI and the shortcut grid

    All nine continuous parameters are automatable and are saved with automation data. They are not in the Automation View parameter list, not on the shortcut grid, and have no default MIDI Follow assignments — but they can be MIDI-learned like any other parameter, and learned mappings persist in SETTINGS/MIDIFollow.XML. Mode and Freeze are not parameters at all, so neither can be automated.

    03The controls

    Values below are the on-screen 0–50 reading. Only Pitch is bipolar; the other eight continuous controls run from bottom to top.

    Mode default OFF

    Which of the six engines is running: Granular, Stretch, Delay, Spectral, Oliverb or Resonestor. Granular, Stretch, Delay and Spectral are stock Clouds; Oliverb and Resonestor came with Parasites.

    OFF is not a mute — it frees the engine's entire working buffer, and costs nothing at all. Changing mode is click-free: the running mode fades out over 10 ms, the engine is rebuilt at silence, and the new mode fades in over 20 ms. Scrolling through the list gives a short dip at each step.

    Blend Blnddefault 0 — fully dry

    Dry/wet, and it means the same thing in all six modes. It starts fully dry deliberately, so that selecting a mode reads as "nothing yet" rather than as an abrupt wall of grains — bring it up to hear the effect at all.

    Blend stays where you set it when you change mode, so you can audition the six modes at the same mix. They are not all equally loud at the same Blend — see Levels in section 05.

    Resonestor uses the same equal-power dry/wet response as the other modes, so Blend 0, 25, and 50 produce a progressive change.

    Position Posncentre 25

    Where in the recording buffer playback reads from — the "when", not the "what". In Delay it is the delay time; in Oliverb a pre-delay; in Spectral the magnitude store/replay position. In Resonestor it shapes an excitation burst that the Deluge never fires, so it does nothing there.

    Size Sizecentre 25

    Grain size in Granular — roughly 16 ms at the bottom to 512 ms at the top. Window size in Stretch, loop length in a frozen Delay, spectral warp in Spectral, room size in Oliverb, and chord selection in Resonestor.

    Pitch Ptchbipolar · centre 25 = unity

    Transposition covers ±24 semitones, two octaves either side of unity, with a centre detent.

    In Delay and Oliverb the pitch shifter has a dead zone by design: below about 0.3 semitones of detune the shifted signal is silent, ramping to full by 0.7 semitones. Small detunes do nothing on purpose.

    Density Densdefault 40 — deliberately off-centre

    In Granular, Density is the grain rate. Around 26–30 it passes through a silent band; the default of 40 stays clear of it.

    In Oliverb, Density is the reverb decay. Up to about 45 the tail just gets longer; above that it self-oscillates and builds without input — the default of 40 is a long, stable tail.

    In the other modes it means something else entirely: diffusion in Stretch and Delay, refresh rate and phase randomisation in Spectral, and resonator feedback in Resonestor — where the law is so steep that essentially all the action is in the top of the travel.

    Texture Textcentre 25

    In Granular, grain window shape — rectangular through gaussian for the first three quarters of the travel, then the remainder becomes diffusion. In Stretch and Delay it is a combined lowpass/highpass tone control sweeping through centre. Spectral quantisation in Spectral, tone in Oliverb, damping and narrowness in Resonestor.

    Spread Sprdcentre 25

    Stereo behaviour, and it differs sharply by mode: per-grain random panning in Granular, a left/right swap-crossfade in Stretch and Delay, diffusion in Oliverb, stereo width and separation in Resonestor. It does nothing at all in Spectral.

    Feedback Fdbkdefault 0 — off

    Regeneration back into the input, with a highpass in the loop, in Granular, Stretch, Delay and Spectral. In Oliverb it is the modulation rate and in Resonestor the harmonicity — in neither of those is it feedback in any sense.

    Reverb Verbdefault 0 — off

    A reverb after the engine, in Granular, Stretch, Delay and Spectral. In Oliverb it is the modulation amount; in Resonestor the spread of the resonator taps. Neither is a reverb.

    Freeze default off · latched

    Freeze latches the current recording buffer. Existing audio keeps playing while new input stops being written.

    Per mode: Granular, Stretch and Delay stop recording, and Delay switches to loop playback with Size as loop length and Pitch as playback speed. Spectral stops capturing magnitudes. Oliverb becomes an infinite hold with the input muted — and is the one mode that keeps recording while frozen. Freeze is hidden while Mode is OFF, where it would do nothing audible.

    The same nine continuous knobs, six ways

    GranularStretchDelaySpectralOliverbResonestor
    Positionread positionplayheaddelay timestore/replay pospre-delayinert
    Sizegrain sizewindow sizeloop length*spectral warproom sizechord
    Pitchgrain transposetransposeshift / speed*shift ratioratio + decaypitch
    Densitygrain ratediffusiondiffusionrefresh + phasedecayfeedback
    Texturewindow shapetonetonequantisationtonedamping
    Spreadgrain panL/R swapL/R swapnothingdiffusionwidth / sep.
    Feedbackfeedbackfeedbackfeedbackfeedbackmod rateharmonicity
    Reverbreverbreverbreverbreverbmod amounttap spread
    Blenddry/wetdry/wetdry/wetdry/wetdry/wetdry/wet

    * when frozen.

    04Starting points

    Six settings worth dialling in as-is, then pulling apart. Values are on-screen 0–50 readings; anything unlisted stays at its default. All of them need Blend brought up — it starts fully dry.

    Grain cloud Granular · Blend 30 · Size 20 · Density 40 · Texture 30

    The sound Wisps is known for. Short grains, randomised triggering, window shape softened. Take Density up for a denser cloud, or into the 26–30 band for silence — which is the dead zone, not a fault.

    Frozen pad Granular · Blend 40 · Size 38 · Density 44 · Freeze on

    Play a chord, switch Freeze on, and the buffer becomes an instrument you can keep grinding after the source has stopped. Position sweeps through what you captured.

    Tape looper Delay · Blend 50 · Position 30 · Feedback 34 · Texture 18

    Position is delay time here, up to about a second. Texture below centre rolls the top off each repeat, so the loop degrades the way tape does.

    Smeared reverb Oliverb · Blend 34 · Size 40 · Density 42 · Spread 32

    Density is decay, Spread is diffusion, Feedback and Reverb are the modulation rate and depth. Add a semitone or two of Pitch for the shimmer.

    Spectral wash Spectral · Blend 36 · Size 25 · Density 25 · Texture 32

    The heaviest mode on the unit — a DSP peak around 90 against Granular's 45, and it runs mono to fit (Clouds' own mono setting; the dry path stays stereo). Density at centre keeps phase coherent; move it either way to randomise. Spread does nothing here.

    Struck resonator Resonestor · Spread 25 · Size 30 · Density 46

    Spread has to stay off its minimum or this mode is silent — at zero the resonator's tap reads are multiplied by nothing. The default of 25 already clears it; the value is listed here because it is the one setting in this recipe you cannot drop to the bottom. Density is the resonator's decay and lives in the top few steps.

    05Defaults, displays and performance

    Defaults and displays

    Control7SEGDefaultSaved asInactive at
    ModeDUSTOffcloudsModeOff — nothing allocated
    BlendBlnd0cloudsBlend0 — fully dry
    PositionPosn25cloudsPosition—

    DensityDens40cloudsDensity— (26–30 is silent)

    Cost by mode

    Measured on the Deluge with SETTINGS → CPU: one instance on a synth, everything at default, Blend 25, the same song each time. DSP samples is the average render, DSP peak the worst; both are the CPU page's own readings, so compare them with the Wisps-off row rather than reading them as a percentage.

    ModeDSP samplesDSP peakWindow peakHard culls
    Wisps OFF (baseline)522—0
    Granular1245250
    Delay1547250
    Resonestor2360290
    Stretch1982350
    Oliverb3482390
    Spectral2691370

    No mode culls on its own. Spectral and Oliverb do their heavy work in the background a slice at a time, spread evenly across renders, which is why their peaks sit near Stretch's rather than far above it. Mode choice matters more than anything else here — and a second instance is not available at all (section 02).

    Rate, and what that costs

    Wisps runs natively at 32 kHz in 16-bit stereo. The Deluge runs at 44.1 kHz. The adapter converts down on the way in, runs the engine in 16-frame blocks, and converts back up, with an exact 441:320 polyphase resampler (Kaiser-windowed sinc filters). The round trip costs 94 samples — about 2.1 ms — and is flat to 13 kHz:

    Frequency100 Hz1 kHz4 kHz10 kHz13 kHz14 kHz15 kHz15.5 kHz
    Level vs the engine itself0.0 dB0.0 dB0.0 dB0.0 dB0.0 dB−0.8 dB−6.1 dB−12 dB
    Aliasing and distortion−65 dB−66 dB−65 dB−64 dB−63 dB−59 dB−25 dB−14 dB

    Note also that the engine's own 32 kHz rate puts Nyquist at 16 kHz regardless of resampler quality. Above 14 kHz the response rolls off by design; Wisps is not the stage to reach for when you want the top octave intact.

    Memory

    The engine needs one 180 KB working buffer. Nothing is allocated while Mode is OFF; the adapter and its buffer are taken as soon as you pick a mode. Selecting OFF again frees the whole thing rather than merely muting it. If the allocation fails you get an insufficient RAM error and the mode reverts to OFF; if the buffer is stolen by the sample cache the recording is lost but audio passes through dry rather than dropping.

    Notes worth keeping in mind

    • Nothing is allocated until you leave OFF. Wisps costs literally nothing while switched off, and selecting OFF gives the 180 KB straight back.
    • Settings survive even when the mode is off. All nine parameters are written unconditionally, so dialling in a texture, switching Wisps off to hear the dry signal, and saving does not lose them. Blend included: switching to OFF and back brings it back where you left it.
    • Levels. All six modes share one wet make-up gain, which puts Stretch and Delay at the dry level. Resonestor's wet return is 6 dB lower, because its resonators ring well above the input when your notes land on their chord. Granular, Spectral and Oliverb build up above dry on held material — that is the cloud, the smear and the tail adding up, not a gain error.
    • Stereo, except Spectral. Two channels in, two out, each with its own recording buffer of about a second. Spectral runs Clouds' own mono setting to fit the CPU: the input is summed to mono for the spectral engine and the result copied to both sides; the dry path stays stereo.
    • Some engine inputs are unavailable from the Deluge controls: Delay tap-tempo trigger, Resonestor excitation trigger, and Spectral glitch. Additional granular sub-parameters remain at fixed values.
    Switching it off entirely

    SETTINGS → COMMUNITY FEATURES → Rudement upgrades → Wisps FX (DUST), on by default. Switching it off hides every Wisps menu but leaves the processing alone, so a song already using Wisps continues to play exactly as saved.

    Tails, and an idle track

    A synth or kit row with Wisps audible keeps rendering after its notes stop, so grains, repeats, tails and a frozen buffer play out rather than being cut off. That costs its CPU for as long as Blend is above 0; Blend at 0 or Mode OFF lets the track go idle again.
