    13MIDI FX
    Synthstrom Deluge · Rudement Firmware
    Chapter 13

    MIDI FX

    Note effects that run whether or not the arpeggiator does

    The note effects run before notes reach a voice or a MIDI socket: velocity, gate time, a drum retrigger, a note delay, a pattern thinner, a chord spreader, a humaniser, a pitch wanderer, a chord follower, and one that writes a part for you. Play FX adds three controls that move the phrase against the clock. All are arp-independent by design — which is why they get their own page group next to the Arpeggiator rather than a corner inside it.

    MIDI FX · Play FX · per clip, per drum

    Your first minute

    #Do thisAnd watch
    1On a synth clip, open the sound menu and turn to MIDI FXThe page group between the Arpeggiator and the Randomizer
    2On Velocity, set Offset to −30 and playEvery note is quieter. 0 is off
    3On a kit, select a drum, open Repeat and set Repeats to 3That drum rolls, even with the transport stopped
    4Look at each page's ResetEdited on the pages you changed, Default on the rest
    5Scroll to Reset all and turn it to DefaultEvery MIDI FX page is back to neutral
    01What it is

    The Deluge already runs every note through the arpeggiator, arp on or off — with the mode off, the arp simply hands the note straight back. That pass-through is where these effects sit, so they work on a held key, on a sequenced note, and on an arpeggiated note alike, without the arp having to be running.

    MIDI FX settings are per clip and saved with the song. Each effect is inactive at its neutral setting and begins working when its own control is moved away from neutral.

    note in (held key, sequencer, or arp output) | Arpeggiator (unchanged; passes through when OFF) | MIDI FX Velocity, Gate, Repeat, Delay, and the note effects in sections 13.1–13.7 | the voice, or the MIDI / CV socket

    Play FX — Clock Shift, Beat Stretch and Division — acts on where the sequencer reads rather than on individual note events. The MIDI FX features are documented in the following sections of this chapter: MIDI Delay is section 13.1, Strum section 13.2, Spread section 13.3, Spice & Dice section 13.4, Stochastic section 13.5, Harmonize section 13.6, and Generate section 13.7. Spice sits directly before Stochastic because both pages show and change the same Roll value.

    02The pages

    MIDI FX sits in the horizontal page strip between the Arpeggiator and the Randomizer, on Synth, MIDI and CV clips, on Kit drums, and on the Kit-global root under AFFECT ENTIRE. Turn to it as you would to Arp; press SELECT to open the group as a list.

    Page7SEGControlsDefault
    VelocityVELOOffset OFST0
    GateGATEGate GATE100%
    RepeatRPTRepeats RPTS, Rate, Decay DECY0 repeats
    DelayDLAYLevel LEVL, Time TIME, Repeats RPTS, FB Vel FBVL, FB Note NOTE, FB Rnd RND, FB Clk FBCL0 / 1/8 / 3 / 0 / 0 / Off / 0
    StrumSTRMTime TIME, Direction DIR, Contour CONT0 / Up / 0
    SpreadSPRDVelocity VELO, Gate GATE, Octave OCTV0 / 0 / 0
    SpiceSPCESpice SPCE, Dice ROLL0 / 0
    StochasticSTOCAmount AMNT, Width WDTH, Dice ROLL0 / 2 / 0
    HarmonizeCHRDFollow Chords FOLO, Chord Track TRACOff
    GenerateGENRDensity DENS, Range RANG, Leap LEAP, Seed SEED, Gate GATE30 / 0 / 25 / 0 / 100%
    Loop RemixLRMXRemix RMX, Type TYPE, Variation VAR, Interval INT— / 1 / Normal 1 / 1
    GrooveGROVTemplate TMPL, Accent ACNT, Time TIME, Random RAND, Offset OFSTOff / 0 / 0 / 0 / 0
    Play FXPFXShift SHFT, Stretch STCH, Division DIVN0 / 100% / 1
    Switching it off entirely

    Set SETTINGS → COMMUNITY FEATURES → Rudement upgrades → MIDI FX to On. This global switch is On by default. Off hides the MIDI FX pages; a song that uses MIDI FX still plays the same. Each effect then uses its own neutral value or dedicated control as described below. Loop Remix and Groove also have their own switches (chapters 14 and 17).

    03Velocity

    One control. Offset, −64 to +63, added to the note's velocity and clamped to 1–127 — never 0, because velocity 0 is note-off on MIDI and emitting one would be a hanging note wearing a disguise.

    With the arpeggiator running, a non-zero offset overrides the arp's velocity spread rather than stacking with it. The effect computes from the note's original velocity so that being run twice on the same note cannot compound it,. At zero it writes nothing at all, so the spread is untouched whenever this is idle.

    04Gate Time

    A ratio on a sequenced note's written length, from a quarter to four times, shown on screen as a percentage.

    The control moves in steps rather than raw percent: zero is neutral, ±12 halves or doubles the length, ±24 is ×0.25 or ×4. One step is a semitone's worth of ratio.

    Two things it deliberately does not do

    A held key passes through untouched. It has no length until it is released, and a percentage of an unknown number is not a thing. It stands down while the arpeggiator runs, because the arp has its own Gate and two gates fighting over one note is not a feature.

    Under 100% the note is released early and the sequencer's own note-off is let through as normal. Over 100% the note is held past its written end, which means the sequencer's note-off has to be suppressed; the note is always released, whether by its timer, the loop point, a retrigger of the same note, or transport stop. An extension shorter than a couple of ticks counts as no extension — taking a note over from the sequencer for nothing is how short notes end up quieter rather than longer.

    05Repeat

    A drum hit repeating itself — Elektron retrig territory, and the reason MIDI FX exists on Kits at all.

    ControlRangeWhat it does
    Repeats0–16How many extra hits follow the original. 0 is off
    Ratesync divisionsThe interval. Triplet and dotted come free, as they do on the arp
    Decay0–100%Velocity multiplier per hit. Below a floor the roll ends rather than emitting velocity 0

    Free-running, not synced. It advances on the audio clock rather than the transport, so hitting a pad with playback stopped still rolls. Four notes can roll at once; a fifth plays undelayed rather than stealing a slot, because a half-emitted roll sounds like a fault rather than a choice.

    06MIDI Delay

    The note repeats at a musical division, each repeat shaped in level, pitch and timing. The controls are described in full in section 13.1.

    Synced, so it is silent with the transport stopped

    The delay runs on the clock, which is what keeps its repeats lined up with everything else. Repeat, above, is the free-running one.

    Releasing the key does not kill the tail — that is the entire point of it. The tail rings across the clip's loop point rather than being cut there. A repeat that fades below velocity 1, or transposes off the end of the keyboard, ends the tail rather than clamping: a clamped tail repeats one pitch forever and reads as a fault.

    Transport stop and clip stop release everything the delay is holding, on MIDI and CV outputs as well as internal voices. That matters more than it sounds: a note this firmware generated and sent out of a MIDI socket is one nothing else in the Deluge knows about, so if the effect does not release it, nothing will.

    07Play FX — Clock Shift, Beat Stretch and Division

    Inspired by the Yamaha RS7000's Play FX, these are the three controls that act on the phrase rather than on note events. They move where the sequencer reads, and touch no notes: nothing is baked in, and recording still records what you played.

    None of the three controls moves anything on screen, and Shift is the one where that surprises people: shift a phrase by most of a bar and the editor looks exactly as it did, because the notes did not move — the place the sequencer reads them from did. All three are judged by ear, and a clip that looks untouched is the feature working rather than a setting that failed to take.

    ControlRangeWhat it does
    Shift−192 to +192 ticksThe phrase plays early or late. A bar either way at the default resolution
    Stretch×0.25 to ×4Fine control of the phrase rate against the clip's length
    Division×8, ×6, ×4, ×3, ×2, 1, /2, /3, /4, /6, /8Sets an exact musical phrase-rate ratio. 1 is neutral

    Division selects an exact musical ratio. Multipliers make the phrase run faster; divisors make it run slower. Division and Stretch multiply together: use Division for the exact musical step and Stretch as the fine adjustment on top of it. Stretch uses the same stepped control as Gate Time, with 100% in the middle. Under 100% the phrase advances faster than the clock and repeats inside the loop; over 100% it advances slower and its tail is truncated at the loop point — which is the behaviour hardware phrase-stretch has always had, and the reason for matching it rather than inventing something kinder.

    Automation deliberately keeps running at the clip's own rate rather than stretching with the notes.

    08On a Kit

    On a Kit the settings are per drum. Select a drum and you edit that drum; hold AFFECT ENTIRE and you edit every drum at once. That rule covers the whole page group, however you reached the menu.

    Play FX is per drum for the same reason and it is the one that makes the case: pushing the hats late against the kick is a thing people want, and shifting the entire kit when one drum is selected is not. On a melodic clip a row is a pitch rather than a drum, so there the three Play FX controls belong to the clip — per-pitch Clock Shift would be a different and much stranger feature.

    Where the value you are looking at comes from

    With a drum selected, the page shows and edits that drum. Under AFFECT ENTIRE with no drum selected, it shows the first drum and writes all of them — after the first turn of the knob they all agree anyway.

    09Reset

    Every page ends with Reset, and the MIDI FX list has Reset all (RALL) at the bottom.

    It reads as well as writes. The value shows Default when that effect is untouched and Edited when it is not, so a pass across the pages tells you which effects are actually doing something — which is the harder half of the problem when a clip does not sound the way you expect. Turning it to Default performs the reset; turning it to Edited does nothing and springs back, because un-reset is not something it can honestly offer.

    It leaves the Community Features switch alone, since that is not a setting of any one effect, and it does not cut a delay tail that is already ringing — that fades out exactly as it would if you turned Repeats to zero by hand. On a Kit, Play FX's Reset clears every drum: a control whose job is getting you back cannot read Default while three other drums are still shifted.

    10Known limits
    Known limits

    Gate Time does nothing to live notes, in either direction. The delay is synced, so it is silent with the transport stopped. There is no shortcut pad; the pages are reached by navigating in.

    ↑ Back to contents
    13.1MIDI Delay
    Synthstrom Deluge · Rudement Firmware
    Section 13.1

    MIDI Delay

    A note that repeats on the clock — fading, rising, or speeding up

    Inspired by the Yamaha RS7000's MIDI delay, this effect makes a note repeat at a musical division, each echo a copy of the last with a little done to it: quieter or louder, shifted in pitch, spaced closer together or further apart. It is locked to the transport rather than free‑running, so the repeats sit on the grid instead of drifting against it — which also means that with the transport stopped, nothing echoes.

    DLAY · MIDI FX → Delay · nothing to switch on

    Your first minute

    #Do thisAnd watch
    1On a synth clip, open MIDI FX → DelayLevel is 0, so the delay is set up but silent
    2Start playback and raise LevelThree echoes, an eighth apart: the defaults
    3Set FB Vel to −20Each echo is quieter than the last
    4Set FB Note to +7Each echo is a fifth higher
    5Stop the transportThe echoes stop. The delay runs on the clock
    01What it is

    Seven controls over one idea. Level sets how loud the echo starts; Time and Repeats set how often and how many; and the four FB controls shape how each repeat differs from the one before it — its volume, its pitch, and the gap in front of it.

    Level is first because it is the knob you ride

    The page opens on Level, and Level defaults to 0. So a fresh clip has the delay already set up — three repeats, an eighth apart — but silent, until you bring the echoes in with one knob. Set the rest on a dead delay, then ride Level to fade it into and out of a phrase.

    Because the echoes are the note's own, they go wherever the note goes: through the synth voice, out over MIDI, or out as CV. An echo can outlive the key that started it — that is the point of a delay — and the effect never hears its own repeats, so a high Repeats count is a long tail, not a runaway.

    02Setting it up

    Keep SETTINGS → COMMUNITY FEATURES → Rudement upgrades → MIDI FX On. This page has no additional Community Features switch. The page is two screens: Level, Time, Repeats on the first, and FB Vel, FB Note, FB Rnd, FB Clk, Reset on the second.

    Control7SEGRangeDefaultWhat it does
    LevelLEVL0–1270The first echo's volume, as a percentage of the note you played: 100 matches it, up to 127 is louder. 0 is silent, so the delay sits armed until you raise it
    TimeTIMEmusical division1/8The interval between repeats. Triplet and dotted divisions come free, and it lines up with the arpeggiator's
    RepeatsRPTS0–643How many echoes follow the note. 0 is off
    FB VelFBVL−127…+1270Added to each repeat's volume: negative fades the tail, positive swells it, 0 holds it level
    FB NoteNOTE−24…+240Semitones added per repeat — a rising or falling delay. 0 is a plain echo
    FB RndRNDOff / OnOffEach repeat takes a fresh random pitch instead of the fixed FB Note step
    FB ClkFBCL−100…+100%0Scales the gap before each successive repeat: negative accelerates the echoes, positive slows them, 0 keeps them on the grid
    ResetRSETDefault / Edited—Reads as well as writes: says at a glance whether the page is doing anything
    03Level and feedback are separate on purpose

    Level sets how loud the echo train starts; FB Vel decides how it evolves. The split is what lets a tail fade or swell rather than only decay: a positive FB Vel makes each repeat louder than the last, which a single “feedback amount” knob cannot do. FB Clk does the same trick for time — a negative value is the bouncing‑ball delay, each gap shorter than the one before.

    A few of these stack into one gesture: set FB Note +7 for rising fifths, or turn FB Rnd on for a scattered cloud. FB Rnd and FB Note work together: with FB Rnd On, each repeat takes a random pitch instead of the fixed FB Note step.

    No switch

    MIDI Delay has no switch of its own. It is part of SETTINGS → COMMUNITY FEATURES → Rudement upgrades → MIDI FX (MIFX, On by default), and it does nothing until you raise Level.

    ↑ Back to contents
    13.2Strum
    Synthstrom Deluge · Rudement Firmware
    Section 13.2

    Strum

    A chord that lands as a sweep

    Every chord you draw on a grid is perfectly simultaneous, which is the one thing no played instrument ever is. Turn Time up and the notes of a chord fire one after another across a few milliseconds instead of together — low to high, high to low, or shuffled — the way a hand crosses guitar strings or a harp. Nothing is rewritten; the chord on the grid is the chord you wrote.

    STRM · MIDI FX → Strum · Off by default

    Your first minute

    #Do thisAnd watch
    1Turn on SETTINGS → COMMUNITY FEATURES → Rudement upgrades → StrumOff by default
    2Put one four-note chord on a step of a synth clip and loop itA block chord
    3Open MIDI FX → Strum and set Time to 8An obvious roll, lowest note first
    4Set Direction to DownThe roll runs the other way
    5Bring Time back to 2–4A natural strum
    01What it is

    The instrument already has three ways to change a chord after you have written it. Spice decides whether each note of it sounds at all; Harmonize decides what pitch each note is; Play FX moves the whole phrase against the clock. None of them touches the internal timing of one chord — the block-ness of it. That is the gap this fills.

    This is the OXI One's timed strum rather than the KeyStep's gesture: you set a gap once and every chord in the clip strums, hands off, while your hands are somewhere else. It is live-adjustable — the spread is read fresh at every chord — so turning the knob during playback changes the next chord, not the one already sounding.

    02Setting it up

    Switch it on once per unit at SETTINGS → COMMUNITY FEATURES → Rudement upgrades → Strum. It ships Off. Then, per clip, MIDI FX → Strum, and turn Time up from 0.

    Control7SEGRangeDefaultWhat it does
    TimeTIME0–24 ticks0The gap between successive notes. 0 is off
    DirectionDIRUp / Down / RandomUpWhich end of the chord sounds first
    ContourCONT−50% to +50%0How far the velocity has moved by the last note of the sweep
    Time is the on/off control

    Strum uses its own neutral value as the off switch: Time 0 is off. Raise Time above 0 to spread a chord.

    There are 48 ticks to a quarter note, so one tick is about 10 ms at 120 bpm. A Time of 1 across three notes is a flam; 6 or 8 across four notes is an unmistakable strum; the top of the range is a slow harp roll. The whole useful range sits in the bottom half of the knob.

    It is tempo-relative, and worth knowing before you change tempo: the strum widens as the tempo drops, because a tick is a fraction of a beat rather than a fixed number of milliseconds. A real strum is physical and does not do that, but most gear that offers this behaves the same way, and an absolute one would need a second timing frame running alongside the transport.

    03What it sounds like when it is working

    Nothing changes on screen. The clip still holds the chord you wrote, on the same step, and the grid, the note editor and the keyboard all keep showing it as a block chord — four notes stacked on one column, exactly as you drew them — however wide the sweep you are hearing. There is no readout that says a strum is happening, so the only confirmation is what you hear — which is worth saying plainly, because the alternative is concluding it is broken while it is working.

    The one-chord test

    Put a single four-note chord on one step of a synth clip, loop it, and set Time to 8 — deliberately too wide. At that setting the chord is an obvious roll rather than a subtlety, so there is no judging it by ear at the threshold. Once you can hear it, walk Time back down to where you actually want it.

    Then set Direction to Down. The roll should turn over and run the other way. That is the proof it is Strum you are hearing and not swing, humanise, or a sloppy quantise setting.

    If nothing is happening at all, it is almost always one of these, in this order:

    CheckWhy
    Time is above 0Time 0 is neutral; raise it above 0 to spread the chord.
    SETTINGS → COMMUNITY FEATURES → Rudement upgrades → Strum is OnIt ships off, and the page still appears and still edits when the toggle is off
    The step actually holds a chordA single note is a chord of one and gets no offset. A melody line is inert by design
    The arpeggiator is off for this clipStrum stands down while the arp runs — see section 06
    The notes are long enoughAn offset is never allowed past a note's own end, so very short notes strum less than you asked for — see section 07
    Spice is not eating the chordWith Spice up, the chord that strums is whatever survived it, which on a thin variation may be one note
    04The order the notes go in

    On a synth, MIDI or CV clip the order is pitch. Up is lowest first, which is a downstroke on a guitar and the one to start with; Down is highest first.

    Random reshuffles every chord, and that is deliberate. Spice's variations repeat bar after bar because a variation is a pattern you are meant to be able to keep; a random strum is a performance gesture, and a hand does not cross the strings the same way twice. Every note still sounds exactly once — it is a shuffle of the order, never a re-roll of which notes play.

    On a Kit, the order is the pad grid

    A kit row is a drum rather than a pitch, so there is nothing to sort by ear. The sweep runs in row order instead — top to bottom of the grid as you are looking at it, so Up starts at the bottom row. A strummed kit chord is a flam, and moving a drum's row moves it in the flam.

    Alternate — up, then down on the next chord — and inward and outward sweeps are not in this version.

    05One setting per clip, kits included

    Velocity, Gate, Repeat, Delay and Spice are all per drum on a Kit — which is right for a repeat, where rolling the snare and not the kick is the point. Strum is not. A flam is a property of the group of drums hitting together rather than of any one of them, and two drums holding different spreads is not a coherent question to ask. So on a Kit there is one set of values for the whole clip.

    SituationWhat happens
    A Kit with no drum selectedThe page stays visible and editable. The other MIDI FX pages hide themselves in that state; this one has nothing to hide behind
    A Kit with one drum selectedYou are still editing the clip's one setting, not that drum's. Select a different drum and the value is the same
    AFFECT ENTIREMeans nothing here, and needs to mean nothing — there is only ever one value to write
    Held under Temp HoldRestored on release like everything else, alongside Play FX, whose values live on the clip in the same place

    The three values are saved with the song.

    06What it composes with
    WithWhat you get
    Spice & DiceSpice thins the chord, then the strum spans whatever survived — so the same written chord strums differently on each variation, and rolling the Dice re-voices the roll
    HarmonizeHarmonize moves the pitches and the strum follows the new voicing. The sweep is ordered by what is actually sounding, not by what is written
    Play FXClock Shift, Beat Stretch and Division move the whole strum as a unit. The chord stays internally spread and arrives early, late or at a different rate
    Gate, Repeat, DelayEach note is an ordinary note by the time they see it, so they act on it exactly as they would unstrummed
    The arpeggiator switches it off

    With the arp running on a clip, Strum stands down for that clip and the arp behaves exactly as it did before this feature existed.

    The reason is worth knowing, because the obvious guess is wrong. The arp does not receive a chord and play it; it builds a set of held notes from the note-ons as they arrive, and plays from the set. Spreading the note-ons therefore does not spread the arp's output — it hands the arp a chord that grows from one note to four over the first few ticks, and changes the pattern it plays. Standing down is the less surprising of the two.

    07Lengths, drones and single notes

    A strummed note keeps every tick of its written length. Its end moves out by exactly as much as its start did, so the chord comes apart at the end as well as at the beginning — which is what a piano does with a rolled chord. A damped guitar ends them together; that is a different sound, and this is not it.

    CaseWhat happens
    A note shorter than its own offsetThe offset is cut down to one tick short of the note — so a very short chord strums as far as it can and no further. It never hangs
    A drone — a note filling its whole rowLeft alone, exactly as Spice leaves it alone. That note is deliberately never stopped at the loop point, so there is no end to move with the start
    A single noteNo offset. This is what keeps the feature inert on a melody line while it is switched on for the clip
    A chord on the last step of the loopThe tail sounds into the next loop. If the new loop retriggers the same rows, whatever is left of the old sweep is dropped rather than doubling the downbeat
    Stopping the clip mid-strumAnything still waiting is dropped rather than fired, and nothing is left ringing

    Nothing is written to the clip. Turning Time back to 0 restores the original playback exactly, and recording a strummed clip onto another track records what is written rather than what you heard.

    08Known limits
    LimitWhat happens
    One tick of resolutionAt 160 bpm a tick is about 7.8 ms, so a three-note chord at Time 1 spans roughly 16 ms. Finer than that is not available
    Tempo-relativeThe strum widens as the tempo drops — see section 02
    Alternate, inward and outwardNot in this version — see section 04
    The arpeggiatorSwitches it off for that clip — see section 06
    No visual feedbackNothing on screen says a strum is happening — see section 03
    Not automatableTime, Direction and Contour are settings rather than parameters, so none of the three has a CC or an automation lane. That is the same trade Spice makes, and it is what lets them work on MIDI and CV clips
    Switching it off entirely

    SETTINGS → COMMUNITY FEATURES → Rudement upgrades → Strum (STRM), Off by default. With it Off the page is still there and still edits, but chords play unstrummed.

    ↑ Back to contents
    13.3Spread
    Synthstrom Deluge · Rudement Firmware
    Section 13.3

    Spread

    The part stops playing itself identically every bar

    A sequenced line is perfectly repeatable, which is most of why it is useful and all of why it can sit dead in a mix. Spread gives every note a little room to move: a few steps of velocity either way, a little more or less gate, and now and then an octave. Nothing is written into the clip — the notes on the grid are the ones you drew, and turning the three controls back to 0 gives you your part back exactly.

    SPRD · MIDI FX → Spread · nothing to switch on

    Your first minute

    #Do thisAnd watch
    1On a synth bassline, open MIDI FX → SpreadAll three at 0: the part plays as written
    2Set Velocity to 12Each note a little louder or softer. Bar 2 matches bar 1
    3Set Gate to 20Notes run a little longer or shorter
    4Set Octave to 15About one note in seven jumps an octave
    5Turn all three back to 0Your part, exactly as written
    01What it is

    Three controls, each pointed at one property of a note that the sequencer otherwise reproduces exactly. They are independent of each other: a note that comes out loud is not therefore long, and the one that jumps an octave is not therefore either.

    Two of the three are spreads and one is a probability

    Velocity and gate are continuous, so “a bit more, a bit less” means something and every note can differ slightly. An octave is not: at ±1 there is no small amount of one, so the only honest control is how often. That is why Octave reads as a percentage chance while the other two read as an amount.

    This is the last of the read-time effects, and it does the job the others leave alone. Spice decides which notes survive at all; Strum decides the internal timing of a chord; Harmonize decides pitch from a chord track. None of them touches how hard, how long, or how high one note lands relative to the same note last time round.

    02Setting it up

    Keep SETTINGS → COMMUNITY FEATURES → Rudement upgrades → MIDI FX On. This page has no additional Community Features switch. All three Spread values use 0 as their neutral setting.

    Control7SEGRangeDefaultWhat it does
    VelocityVELO0–64 steps0How far either side of the written velocity a note may land
    GateGATE0–90%0How far either side of its written length a note may run
    OctaveOCTV0–100%0How often a note is thrown an octave, up or down
    ResetRSETDefault / Edited—Reads as well as writes: says at a glance whether this page is doing anything

    Useful starting points, and they are lower than you would guess: Velocity 8–16, Gate 15–30, Octave 10–25. Past those the part stops sounding like a part played loosely and starts sounding like a part played badly, which is a different and less useful thing.

    Not on Kits — the page is not there

    On a Kit clip there is no Spread page at all, and that is deliberate rather than unfinished. A kit row's loudness is already randomisable from the patch matrix by patching master volume to Random, and an octave means nothing on a row that is a drum rather than a pitch. A page offering three controls of which one duplicates the matrix and two do nothing would be worse than no page. Synth, MIDI and CV clips only.

    03Velocity — in steps, not percent

    The number is absolute velocity steps. At 10, a note written at 64 lands somewhere between 54 and 74, and a note written at 110 lands between 100 and 120. Both wander by the same amount.

    That is the whole reason it is not a percentage, and it matters on any part you have already shaped. A proportional spread of 15% would move a written 110 by up to 16 and a written 30 by up to 4 — so your accents would wander four times as far as your ghost notes, and the dynamic shape you drew would be swamped by the variation meant to sit underneath it. Absolute steps leave that shape intact.

    It never reaches 0

    Velocity 0 is a note-off in MIDI, so a spread that could reach it would be a silent note at best and a hanging one at worst. The floor is 1 and the ceiling is 127, both clamped. At Velocity 40 on a quiet part you will hear that clamping as the bottom of the range flattening out; that is the control being run past its useful end rather than a fault.

    It is applied to the written velocity, before Strum's Contour tilts the chord. So a strummed chord still fades or swells across the sweep the way you set it; it just does not do so from identical starting points each time.

    04Gate — the only one of the three that goes both ways

    A percentage of each note's written length, either side of it. At 30, a note written four steps long plays between about two and a half and five and a bit.

    Worth being plain about the difference from Spice's gate, because they look similar on the menu and are not. Spice only ever shortens, which makes a part drier — you hear it as the phrase getting shorter. Spread goes both ways, which makes a part looser. On a pad or a held bass the lengthening half is most of what you are buying: notes that run into each other by a tick or two, unevenly, is a great deal of what separates a played line from a drawn one.

    A lengthened note is clamped against the next one in its row

    Two notes overlapping in one row is not a state the sequencer permits, so a note that would run into the next one is cut back to meet it rather than stretched over it. At high settings on a busy line you will therefore hear the long half of the range doing less than the short half — there is simply nowhere for the note to go. On a sparse part, where there is room, the effect is symmetric.

    Notes filling their whole row — drones — are left alone entirely, for the same reason Spice leaves them alone: they are meant to run into the next loop and have no note-off to move.

    05Octave — a chance, not a range

    This is the one that changes a part rather than seasoning it, and it is the reason the page is worth having on a bassline. At 15%, roughly one note in seven jumps — up or down, the firmware picks — and the rest play as written. That is the octave-pop bassline, a gesture you notice and could sing back.

    The arpeggiator's Randomizer page spells this the other way

    That page has Spread Velocity, Spread Gate and Spread Octave too, and the names here are borrowed from it on purpose so that anyone who knows that page knows this one. One difference: there, Spread Octave is a range the arp picks within. Here it is a chance. Also worth knowing: those fourteen Randomizer parameters do nothing at all with the arpeggiator switched off, which is exactly the gap this page fills.

    Jumps are ±1 octave only. Wider scatter stops sounding like a line and starts sounding like an accident, and Generate's Range already does deliberate wide movement better.

    At the edges of the keyboard a jump that would leave the note range simply does not happen — the note plays where it was written. It is not clamped to the lowest note, which would pile several notes onto one pitch and sound like a fault, and it is not dropped, which would put a hole in the phrase. So near the bottom of a bassline you will find the down-jumps quietly stop occurring and the up-jumps carry on, which is what you want there anyway.

    06Why there is no Dice

    Spice has a Dice knob for browsing different rolls of the same pattern, and this page deliberately does not. Spice makes patterns, and auditioning variations of a pattern is the point of it. This is an amount — nobody sits and browses alternative versions of humanisation.

    What that buys you is worth knowing, because it is the same property Spice's Dice has and for the same reason. The variation is computed from the note's row and its position in the bar, not drawn from a random generator, so:

    What you doWhat happens
    Let the clip loopBar 2 is identical to bar 1. The variation is part of the groove rather than a wobble laid over it
    Stop and restart playbackThe same. Nothing is re-rolled at the downbeat
    Save the song and load it tomorrowThe same again. Nothing per note is stored to make this work
    Move a note to a different stepThat note gets a different value — its position is part of the sum
    Move a row, or copy the part to another rowThe whole row gets a different set. The row is part of the sum too, which is what stops a chord's notes all moving together

    If you want the loop to actually differ bar to bar, the tool for that is Spice, whose Dice you can turn while it plays.

    07What it composes with
    WithWhat happens
    HarmonizeThe octave lands after the chord tone is chosen, so a displaced note is still in the chord. Doing it the other way round would throw the octave away, because Harmonize derives the pitch from the written note's scale degree
    StrumThey stack. The chord spreads in time, and each note of it also lands at its own velocity and length
    SpiceThey stack, and the order is: Spice decides what survives, then this varies what is left. The gate halves compose — Spice shortens, then this varies the result
    The arpeggiatorAll three reach the arp, because they are applied before the arpeggiator. An arpeggiated part gets varied velocities and the occasional displaced octave
    Velocity and Gate on the MIDI FX pagesDifferent jobs, and they compose. Those two offset every note by a fixed amount; these vary each note around whatever it already is
    Recording this clip onto another trackRecords what is written, not what you heard. Nothing here is baked in
    Temp HoldNot held. A Spread change made while SHIFT is held stays when you let go
    08Known limits
    LimitWhat happens
    Not on KitsThe page does not appear there — see section 02
    No timing spreadNote positions are untouched. Spread does not push notes off the grid; nudging and Strum are the tools for timing
    Nothing on screenThe grid keeps showing the part as written, because that is what it still is. As with Strum, the confirmation is what you hear
    Clip-wide, not per rowOne set of three values for the whole clip. A part where the bass should wander and the lead should not wants two clips
    Octave is ±1 onlyBy design — see section 05
    Not automatableThe three are settings rather than parameters, so none has a CC or an automation lane. That is the same trade Spice and Strum make, and it is what lets them work on MIDI and CV clips

    The three values are saved with the song.

    No switch

    Spread has no switch of its own. It is part of SETTINGS → COMMUNITY FEATURES → Rudement upgrades → MIDI FX (MIFX, On by default), and it does nothing while its three values are 0.

    ↑ Back to contents
    13.4Spice & Dice
    Synthstrom Deluge · Rudement Firmware
    Section 13.4

    Spice & Dice

    Thinning a written phrase without writing anything

    Two knobs borrowed from Arturia's MicroFreak. Spice is how far the gates wander from what you wrote; Dice is which variation you are hearing. Between them they give one written pattern a hundred versions of itself, none of which alter the pattern.

    SPCE · ROLL · per clip, per drum

    Your first minute

    #Do thisAnd watch
    1On a busy drum or synth clip, open MIDI FX → SpiceSpice 0, Dice 0: plays as written
    2Set Spice to 25Some steps drop and some gates shorten, the same way every bar
    3Turn Dice a few clicksA different variation at each click, held until you move it again
    4Turn Dice back to where you startedThe first variation returns exactly
    5Set Spice back to 0The pattern as written
    01What it is

    A sequenced pattern repeats exactly, bar after bar. The Deluge already carries one answer to that in per-note probability — mark a step 50% and it plays half the time — but that is a different thing, because it re-rolls every bar. The result is an unstable pattern rather than a second pattern.

    Spice produces the second pattern. Turn it up and steps start dropping out while surviving notes get shorter gates; turn Dice and a different set of drops appears, and holds until Dice moves again. Turn Spice back to 0 and the clip plays exactly as written, because it always was written that way — see section 03.

    02The two controls

    Spice is a page in the MIDI FX group, between Spread and Stochastic — on Synth, MIDI and CV clips, on Kit drums, and on the Kit-global root under AFFECT ENTIRE. It is reached the way the rest of that group is: turn to MIDI FX in the horizontal page strip and press SELECT.

    Control7SEGRangeWhat it doesDefault
    SpiceSPCE0–50How far the gates wander. At 0 the clip plays as written; at 50 a little over half the steps are gone0
    DiceROLL0–99Which variation. Turning this knob is the roll0
    ResetRSET—Back to 0 / 0, and reads Default or Edited like every other Reset in the group—

    Spice climbs to 50 rather than 100 because the useful range runs out once about half the notes are gone: a phrase with everything missing is silence, not a variation. The drop chance and the gate shortening move together on the one knob, so there is one thing to turn rather than two that have to be balanced against each other.

    Both save with the song. A variation returns intact on reload, on the same Dice number. That is also why Dice is a plain number rather than a hidden seed: it can be read off the screen and written down.

    03Nothing is written into the clip

    Both halves are read at playback time. The notes, their lengths, their probabilities and their conditions are untouched — Spice decides what to do with each note as the sequencer reaches it, and decides again next bar.

    Three things follow from that, and they are the reason it was built this way:

    What happens
    Turning Spice back to 0The original sequence is intact. There is nothing to undo
    Opening the clip in the editorThe editor shows the written pattern, not the one just heard
    Recording a spiced clip into the arrangerThe written pattern is what records. Nothing bakes in

    Recording keeps the written pattern so that a spiced take never overwrites the part by accident. To keep a performance exactly as it sounded, resample the audio output.

    04A hash, not a roll

    Whether a step drops, and how short its gate becomes, are pure functions of three numbers: the Dice value, which row the note is on, and where in the clip it sits. Nothing is stored per note, and there is no random-number state anywhere.

    That is what makes the variation a variation. It survives the loop point, a clip relaunch, and a stop and start.

    The row goes into the hash so that the rows of a kit do not drop in lockstep. Without it every row makes the same decision at the same step, the whole kit stutters as one block, and the result reads as a dropout rather than as a groove. Whether a step drops and how short its gate gets are decided separately, so surviving notes do not all come out the same length.

    05On a Kit

    Per drum, like the rest of MIDI FX. Select a drum and that drum is spiced; hold AFFECT ENTIRE and the whole kit is spiced at once.

    Even then each row still decides for itself, because the row is in the hash. A kit at Spice 30 thins out — a hat missing here, a snare missing there — rather than dropping whole beats. That is the difference between a groove and a fault.

    06Rolling without looking

    SETTINGS → MIDI → COMMANDS → Dice learns a note, a CC or a program change, the same way the transport commands do. A footswitch or a spare pad then rolls a new variation without a trip into the menus.

    It is song-wide. A footswitch has no way to say which track it meant, so one press moves everything that is spiced to the same new variation — every melodic clip and every drum of every kit. Tracks sitting at Spice 0 are left alone, so the command is only as broad as the spicing you have set up.

    One press always lands somewhere new

    The command remembers the number it last handed out and will not hand out the same one twice in a row. A press that produces no change is indistinguishable from a press that did not register, and an unreliable control is worse than no control.

    It is momentary: there is nothing to hold, and the note-off does nothing. Everything that was spiced still decides row by row, so the song turns a corner together without moving in lockstep.

    07Order of operations

    Spice runs last, and it only ever subtracts.

    the note as written | probability / iterance / fill condition (unchanged) | Spice may drop it, may shorten it | the voice, or the MIDI / CV socket

    A note that failed its own condition stays failed — the dice never resurrects anything a condition was explicitly written for. FILL notes are never dropped by Spice: a fill is already a deliberate performance gesture, and thinning it out would be Spice arguing with a decision you made on purpose.

    Spiced notes go out of the MIDI and CV sockets as well as to the internal voice, because they all leave by the same door. On a MIDI clip that means Spice thins the pattern reaching the external gear, which is the point of it being here rather than a side effect of where it was built.

    08Known limits
    Known limits

    Gates only shorten; they do not lengthen. Use Gate Time above 100% when a note must continue past its written end. Silent steps remain silent, and drones are left unchanged. Spice is saved with each clip or drum and works on Synth, MIDI, CV and Kit clips. It has no gold-knob parameter, automation lane, or dedicated CC; Dice provides the global MIDI command for performance control.

    No switch

    Spice & Dice has no switch of its own. It is part of SETTINGS → COMMUNITY FEATURES → Rudement upgrades → MIDI FX (MIFX, On by default), and it does nothing while Spice is 0.

    ↑ Back to contents
    13.5Stochastic
    Synthstrom Deluge · Rudement Firmware
    Section 13.5

    Stochastic

    The rhythm you wrote, with the pitches drawn afresh

    A written phrase plays the same notes in the same order for as long as you let it run, and there is a particular kind of part — a generative one — that wants the opposite. Stochastic keeps every step, length and accent exactly where you drew it and lets some of the pitches move: a scale degree or two either way, on some notes and not others, in a pattern you can browse and come back to. The second of the OXI One's three generative modes, and the other half of what Spice does.

    STOC · MIDI FX → Stochastic · nothing to switch on

    Your first minute

    #Do thisAnd watch
    1Make sure the song has a scale, then open MIDI FX → Stochastic on a synth melodyAmount 0: plays as written
    2Set Amount 30, Width 2Two or three notes a bar move to nearby scale notes, always in key
    3Let it loopBar 2 is the same as bar 1
    4Turn DiceA different set of moves. Spice's Dice changes too: it is the same number
    5Set Amount back to 0Your phrase returns exactly
    01What it is

    Spice locks the pitch and varies the gate: the notes are the ones you wrote, and which of them survive changes. This does the reverse. The rhythm is locked — every note you drew still fires, at the length and velocity you gave it — and the pitch is drawn afresh.

    Two controls, because “how often” and “how far” are different questions

    Amount is the chance that a given note is redrawn at all. Width is how far it may go when it is. One combined knob could only ever give a constant shimmer at its low settings — it could never give "my part, mostly as written, with the occasional departure", which is the setting most people actually want and is roughly Amount 30 at Width 2.

    Nothing is written into the clip. The grid holds the phrase you drew, and turning Amount back to 0 gives it back exactly — the same contract Spice, Strum, Harmonize and Spread all keep.

    02Setting it up

    Keep SETTINGS → COMMUNITY FEATURES → Rudement upgrades → MIDI FX On. This page has no additional Community Features switch. Stochastic Amount 0 is its neutral setting.

    Control7SEGRangeDefaultWhat it does
    AmountAMNT0–100%0How many of the written notes are redrawn
    WidthWDTH1–7 degrees2How far a redrawn note may move, either side of where it is written
    DiceROLL0–990Which variation. This is Spice's Dice — see section 06
    ResetRSETDefault / Edited—Reads as well as writes: says at a glance whether this page is doing anything

    Useful starting points: Amount 25–40 with Width 2 for a part that is recognisably still yours, and Amount 70–100 with Width 4 or more when you want the phrase to be a rhythm carrying a tune you did not write. At Amount 100 every note moves — a redrawn note never lands back where it started, so the top of the knob means what it says.

    Not on Kits — the page is not there

    On a Kit, each row represents a drum rather than a pitch, so Stochastic is available on Synth, MIDI, and CV clips only.

    03What it sounds like when it is working

    Nothing changes on screen. The grid, the note editor and the keyboard all keep showing the phrase you wrote, on the pitches you wrote it on, because that is still what the clip holds. This page acts at read time. If you set it up correctly and then look for confirmation, there is none to find, and the reasonable conclusion is that it is broken.

    So judge it by ear, and here is what to listen for. With Amount at 30 and Width at 2, a four-bar loop should sound like your part, with two or three notes per bar sitting somewhere you did not put them — near neighbours, in key, never sour. Bar 2 should be identical to bar 1 rather than different: the variation is part of the groove, not a wobble laid over it.

    The one-knob proof

    Turn Amount from 0 to 100 and back while it loops. At 100 the melody is unrecognisable and still in key; at 0 your phrase returns exactly. If both ends do what they should, it is working — and if the two ends sound the same, see section 08.

    04Degrees, not semitones

    Width counts in degrees of the song's key, not semitones. Width 1 moves a note to the next note of the scale, up or down — which is two semitones in some places and one in others, and that is the point. The result is in key by construction rather than by correction, and it follows the song: change the scale and the same Dice gives you the same shape in the new key.

    The alternative — draw semitones, then snap whatever comes out to the nearest scale note — is in key only by accident, and it bunches. Two or three different draws snap onto the same pitch, so the result leans on whichever notes the snap happens to favour and the part develops a stutter nobody wrote.

    A note outside the key never moves

    Write a chromatic passing note and it stays exactly where it is, at any Amount. A note with no degree has nothing to add an offset to, and moving it by “two degrees” would mean moving it by some arbitrary interval. You put that note there on purpose, so it is left alone. (Harmonize answers the same question differently — it snaps an out-of-key note to the nearest chord tone — which is right for a harmoniser and wrong here.)

    Width tops out at 7, an octave of a seven-note scale. Past that the contour of what you wrote stops being audible underneath the wander, and what you want instead is Generate, which writes a line rather than bending one.

    05Where it sits in the chain

    The order matters, because it is what makes Stochastic work with the rest of the group.

    written note | Stochastic picks a degree, a step or two either way | Harmonize maps that degree onto a tone of the chord track's chord | Spread may throw it an octave | the voice, or the MIDI / CV socket

    The wander happens first, and everything downstream treats its result as though you had written it. That is the whole design. Run the two the other way round — harmonise, then wander — and Harmonize's careful work is undone one step later by a shift of two scale degrees, and a generative clip simply plays notes that are not in the chord.

    06The Dice is Spice's Dice

    There is one Dice for the group, not one per page. Turn it on the Stochastic page and the Spice page reads the same number, because it is the same number — one value answering “which variation am I hearing” across everything that varies.

    That is the better model of the two, and it has a consequence worth knowing before it surprises you: browsing pitch variations here also re-rolls your Spice gates. If you have found a thinning you like and you now want a different set of pitches over it, there is no way to move one without the other. If you want them independent, use two clips.

    What the shared Dice buys is the same property Spice's has, for the same reason. The variation is computed from the note's row, its position in the bar and the Dice number — not drawn from a random generator — so:

    What you doWhat happens
    Let the clip loopBar 2 is identical to bar 1
    Stop and restart playbackThe same. Nothing is re-rolled at the downbeat
    Save the song and load it tomorrowThe same again. Nothing per note is stored to make this work
    Turn Dice up two and back down twoExactly the phrase you had. A variation you liked is never lost
    Move a note to a different stepThat note draws differently — its position is part of the sum
    Transpose the rowThe whole row draws differently. The row is part of the sum too
    07What it composes with
    WithWhat happens
    HarmonizeEvery wandered note is still a tone of the chord — section 05. This is the pairing the feature exists for: the chord track holds the harmony, this holds the invention
    SpiceThe obvious partner. Spice thins the rhythm, this moves the pitches, and one Dice browses both at once
    SpreadRuns after. An octave of a chord tone is still a chord tone, so the three stack cleanly
    StrumThey stack. A chord whose notes have wandered still lands as a sweep
    The arpeggiatorArpeggiates the wandered notes with no effort at all — the pitch is decided before the arpeggiator
    GenerateDifferent jobs, and they compose well: Generate writes a part into the clip, this bends the part that is there. Generate once, then wander it, and undo still takes the generation back out
    Recording this clip onto another trackRecords what is written, not what you heard. Nothing here is baked in
    Temp HoldNot held. A Stochastic change made while SHIFT is held stays when you let go
    08If it is not doing anything

    In the order each is actually the problem.

    CheckWhy
    Amount is above 0Amount 0 is neutral; raise it above 0 to move notes.
    The clip is not a KitThe page is not there at all on a Kit — if you cannot find it, that is why
    The song has a scaleThe wander counts in degrees of the song's key. With no scale to count in, the page stands down rather than guessing
    The notes are in that keyOut-of-key notes never move — section 04. A phrase written chromatically will sit there unchanged at Amount 100
    You are listening, not lookingThe grid shows the written phrase and always will — section 03
    The part is not one repeated noteIt still works, but a wander of a monotone at Width 2 is hard to hear as anything but a slightly different monotone. Give it a phrase with shape
    09Known limits
    LimitWhat happens
    Not on KitsThe page does not appear there — see section 02
    The Dice is sharedBrowsing variations here re-rolls Spice's gates too — see section 06
    Notes at the edge of the keyboardA wander that would leave the note range is declined, not clamped: a bassline sitting on the floor simply stops making its downward jumps. Clamping would pile several notes onto one pitch, which is heard as a fault
    Clip-wide, not per rowOne Amount and one Width for the whole clip. A part where the bass should stay put and the lead should wander wants two clips
    Nothing on screenBy design, and the reason section 03 exists
    Not automatableAmount and Width are settings rather than parameters, so neither has a CC or an automation lane. The Dice does have a global MIDI command, which reaches this page too — see chapter 23
    Width is in degreesSo its size in semitones depends on the scale. Seven degrees of a pentatonic is not seven degrees of a major scale

    Amount and Width are saved with the song.

    No switch

    Stochastic has no switch of its own. It is part of SETTINGS → COMMUNITY FEATURES → Rudement upgrades → MIDI FX (MIFX, On by default), and it does nothing while Amount is 0.

    ↑ Back to contents
    13.6Harmonize
    Synthstrom Deluge · Rudement Firmware
    Section 13.6

    Harmonize

    A phrase that follows the chords

    Nominate one track as the chord track. Any other clip you switch Follow Chords on for stops playing its written pitches and plays its written shape instead — each note becoming a tone of whatever chord is sounding at that moment. The rhythm, the phrasing and the contour are exactly as you wrote them. Only the pitches move, and they move with the progression.

    CHRD · MIDI FX → Harmonize · Off by default

    Your first minute

    #Do thisAnd watch
    1Turn on SETTINGS → COMMUNITY FEATURES → Rudement upgrades → HarmonizeOff by default
    2Make a chord track with two bars of different chords, and give the track a nameThis is the track that will steer
    3On a melody clip, open MIDI FX → Harmonize → Chord Track and pick itThe source is set for the whole song
    4Set Follow Chords to OnThe melody plays chord tones and moves with each chord
    5Mute the chord trackThe melody keeps following chords you can no longer hear
    01What it is

    The Deluge already keeps a whole song in one key. That keeps you in key; it does not keep you in chord. A bassline written over A minor plays the same four notes when the progression moves to F, and three of them are now the wrong three.

    This is the missing half, and it is the OXI One's HARMO scale by another name. Write the line once, against the chords you happen to have, and it stays right as the chords move underneath it.

    02Setting it up

    Three things have to be true, and the first one is once per unit rather than once per song.

    StepWhere
    Turn the feature onSETTINGS → COMMUNITY FEATURES → Rudement upgrades → Harmonize. Ships off
    Name the chord trackOn the clip that will follow: MIDI FX → Harmonize → Chord Track, and pick the track holding your chords
    Turn it on for the clip you want to follow the chordsMIDI FX → Harmonize → Follow Chords = On

    Chord Track is song-wide; Follow Chords is per clip. You set the source once and then switch clips over to it one at a time. The picker lives on the Harmonize page because that is where you are standing when you want it, not because it belongs to that clip.

    What turns Harmonize on

    Follow Chords is the per-clip on/off control. Chord Track selects the song-wide source.

    On a 7-segment display the page reads CHRD, and its two entries read FOLO and TRAC. HARM is already used by the Chroma layout and by Bouls Harmonics.

    03What it sounds like when it is working

    Nothing changes on screen. The grid, the note editor and the keyboard all keep showing the notes you wrote, because that is what is still in the clip — so the only confirmation is what you hear. Looking for a visual cue and not finding one is the first way this feature reads as broken when it is working perfectly.

    What to listen for: the phrase keeps its rhythm exactly — same hits, same lengths, same accents — while its pitches move as the chord track changes chord. If the rhythm changed, something else did that, not this.

    The two-bar test

    Put a bar of one chord and a bar of another on the chord track, and a short line on the follower. Run them together: the line should sit where you wrote it over the first bar and come out on different notes over the second, with its shape intact.

    Then mute the chord track. The line should carry on following the progression with the chords silent. That is the part no other setting on the instrument does, so it is the proof that Harmonize is what you are hearing.

    If nothing is happening at all, it is almost always one of these four things, in this order:

    CheckWhy
    Chord Track is actually set, not OffWith no chord track there is nothing to follow, and the clip plays as written
    The chord track has a nameAn unnamed track cannot be stored or chosen — see section 05
    The follower is not the chord track itselfA clip harmonised to its own track is ignored
    The follower is not a KitKits are out, and the page hides itself there — see section 06
    04How a note is chosen

    Every note is read as a degree — how far up the song's scale it sits from the key root — and that degree picks a tone of the chord. The root of the key plays the chord's lowest note, the next step up plays the next chord tone, and so on; past the top of the chord it wraps to the bottom an octave higher.

    Two consequences are worth knowing before you judge it by one clip.

    What you wroteWhat you get
    A stepwise runAn arpeggio of the chord. Four scale steps are four chord tones, not four semitone-accurate steps
    A leap of an octaveStill an octave. The written octave is carried straight through
    A note outside the song's keySnapped to the nearest chord tone rather than dropped — a passing note stays a passing note
    Two rows landing on one pitchThe second is bumped up to the next chord tone, so nothing doubles and no voice is lost

    The scale that decides the degrees is the song's, at SETTINGS → SCALE — so a phrase written in a scale the song is not in reads as a run of out-of-key notes and gets the snapped treatment throughout. That sounds like a thinner version of the feature rather than like a fault, which is the failure worth recognising.

    05The chord track

    The chord track is a track, not a clip: whichever clip of it is playing supplies the chords, so launching a different clip on that track changes the progression and nothing has to be re-pointed.

    SituationWhat happens
    The chord track is mutedIt still steers. Mute the chords so nobody hears them and everything following them carries on
    A single row of the chord clip is mutedThat note leaves the chord. A muted row is a note you took out; a muted track is a track you turned down
    Between chords, or the chord track stoppedThe last chord is held. A phrase does not jump back to its written pitches for the length of a rest
    Nothing has played yet on the chord trackThe clip plays as written until the first chord arrives
    A clip harmonised to its own trackIgnored. It plays as written

    Up to eight notes at once count as the chord; more than that is not a chord, and the extras are left out.

    Renaming the chord track unhooks it

    The setting is stored as the track's name, which is what survives adding, deleting and reordering tracks — the things that break a stored position. The price is that renaming the chord track leaves the setting pointing at a name that no longer exists, and the followers quietly play as written. The fix is to open Chord Track and pick it again.

    A track with no name cannot be chosen at all, for the same reason: there is nothing to store.

    The choice is saved with the song, so a song reloads pointing at the same chord track.

    06What it does and does not touch

    Nothing is rewritten. The clip on the grid is the clip you wrote, always. Harmonize exists only in the moment a note is sent, so switching it off returns the phrase to its written pitches with nothing to undo — and the grid, the note editor and the keyboard keep showing what you wrote rather than what is sounding.

    ReachesDetail
    Synth, MIDI and CV clipsThe re-pitch happens before the note leaves the sequencer, so external gear is harmonised as readily as an internal synth
    The arpeggiatorFree. An arpeggiated harmonised clip arpeggiates the harmonised notes
    The rest of MIDI FXFree, for the same reason — Repeat, Delay and Gate all act on the harmonised pitch
    Spice & DiceComposes with it. Spice decides whether a step sounds and how long; this decides what pitch
    What it does not reach

    Kits are out. A kit row is a drum rather than a pitch, so harmonising one would change which drum played; the page hides itself on a kit. A note already sounding is not re-pitched. A chord change under a long held note leaves that note where it started and takes effect on the next note — a note whose pitch moved halfway through would have to be stopped and restarted, and a note that is stopped at the wrong moment is a stuck note.

    07Known limits
    LimitWhat happens
    One chord track per songTwo progressions at once is not available. Every following clip reads the same source
    Held notesNot re-pitched mid-note — see section 06
    KitsThe page does not appear
    A renamed chord trackSilently unhooks — see section 05
    Notes below the key rootFollow the chord's own voicing, so a low phrase can sit higher than written if the chord track is voiced high. Transposing the chord track down moves the followers with it
    Switching it off entirely

    SETTINGS → COMMUNITY FEATURES → Rudement upgrades → Harmonize (CHRD), Off by default. Off: every clip plays its written pitches. Follow Chords and Chord Track stay saved in the song.

    ↑ Back to contents
    13.7Generate
    Synthstrom Deluge · Rudement Firmware
    Section 13.7

    Generate

    The sequencer writes the part, you edit it

    A blank clip and no idea is a worse problem than a wrong idea. Generate fills a row — or a run of rows — with a pattern built inside limits you set: how busy, how wide, how much it jumps. What it writes is ordinary notes on the grid, yours to nudge, re-length, thin or throw away. It is the one thing in the MIDI FX group that changes the clip rather than changing how the clip is played.

    GENR · MIDI FX → Generate · nothing to switch on

    Your first minute

    #Do thisAnd watch
    1On a synth clip, tap a row's audition padThat row is the target
    2Open MIDI FX → Generate, set Density 30, Range 0Nothing yet: the settings change nothing on their own
    3Press SELECT on Generate nowA rhythm appears on that row, and the display says how many notes landed
    4Turn Seed and press Generate now againA different rhythm replaces the first
    5Set Range to 7 and generateA melody over the same groove. Undo from clip view takes it back
    01What it is
    This one writes — everything else in the group does not

    Every other MIDI FX page — Velocity, Gate, Repeat, Delay, Strum, Spread, Spice, Stochastic, Harmonize, Loop Remix and Groove — is a read-time effect: the clip on the grid stays exactly as you wrote it, and turning the effect off gives your phrase back untouched. Generate replaces the notes. It goes through the undo log like any other edit, and undo — not a knob — is how you get back. That difference is the whole reason it is worth reading a page about.

    Two things are being decided, and it is worth keeping them apart in your head because the controls do. When notes happen — which steps carry a note at all — and what pitch each of those notes takes. Density, Seed and Gate decide the first; Range and Leap decide the second.

    They are independent on purpose. Find a rhythm you like at Range 0, then turn Range up and a tune appears over that same groove rather than instead of it. Turn it back down and the groove is still there.

    02Picking the row it writes into

    This is the part that catches people, and it is worth getting right before touching any of the controls. Generate writes into one target row, and when Range is up it climbs from that row upward. It never asks which row; it uses the one you last touched.

    Clip typeThe target isHow you set it
    Synth, MIDI, CVThe row whose audition pad you last tappedTap that row's audition pad before opening the menu
    KitThe selected drum — the one litTap that drum's pad once

    The two are different on purpose. On a Kit the selected drum is the row the rest of the MIDI FX group is already scoped to, so Generate agrees with the page you are standing on; a kit row is also a drum rather than a pitch, so there is no row above it to climb to.

    If it says Select a drum or note row first

    It could not work out where to write, and refused rather than guessing. On a Kit, tap a drum pad. On a synth clip, tap an audition pad. It also refuses at Density 0 — see section 03 — and it only works from clip view, not from Song view or the arranger.

    03Setting it up

    Keep SETTINGS → COMMUNITY FEATURES → Rudement upgrades → MIDI FX On. This page has no additional Community Features switch. Generate runs as a command when you confirm it.

    Control7SEGRangeDefaultWhat it does
    DensityDENS0–10030How likely each step is to carry a note
    RangeRANG0–24 degrees0How far above the target row the line may climb. 0 keeps every note in that one row
    LeapLEAP0–10025How often the line jumps rather than stepping to the next note of the scale
    SeedSEED0–990Which pattern. Not a dice roll — see section 04
    GateGATE5–200%100Note length, as a percentage of one step
    Generate nowGO——Writes it. Nothing happens until you press this

    Turning any of the five changes nothing on its own, so you can set the page up in full before committing to anything. The display reports how many notes landed.

    Density 0 refuses; it does not empty the row

    A generator that silently deleted your part because a knob was left at the bottom is not one you would reach for twice. Clearing a row is what CLEAR is for.

    The step grid is the one you are looking at, the same as the Euclidean edit uses, so zoom in for a finer pattern and out for a coarser one.

    04The seed is a number, not a dice roll

    A given Seed always creates the same pattern for the same row and settings. You can return to a previous Seed and recover the same result.

    What you doWhat happens
    Turn Seed, press Generate now, listenA different part, from the same settings
    Don't like it — turn Seed againAnother one. Keep going; there are a hundred
    Liked the one three turns backTurn back to that number and generate. It is the same part, exactly

    Nothing is stored per note to make this work — the pattern is recomputed from the number every time it is asked for, which is the same trick Spice's Dice uses and why both of them cost nothing to save with a song.

    The seed is combined with the row

    The same Seed number gives a different pattern on each row, which is what you want on a kit: set every drum to seed 4 and you get four different parts rather than four copies of one. It is also why moving a drum to a different row changes what that seed generates there.

    One more property worth knowing, because it is the opposite of what you might expect. Zoom in a level and generate again at the same seed: the notes that were already there stay where they are and new ones appear between them. The pattern refines rather than reshuffling, because each step's decision is tied to its position in the bar rather than to its number in the row.

    05Drums — leave Range at 0

    A kit row is a drum, not a pitch. A line climbing through rows would walk across your kit rather than up a scale, so Range is ignored on a Kit whatever the knob says, and everything lands in the drum you selected.

    That makes the drum workflow three controls and a loop: tap a drum, set Density, press Generate now, then turn Seed until you like what you hear. Tap the next drum and do it again. Because the seed is combined with the row, you can leave Seed where it is and still get a different pattern on the next drum.

    SettingOn drums
    Density 10–20Sparse — a kick or an accent that leaves room
    Density 30–50A working hat or snare part
    Density 70+A roll. Useful on one row, tiring across a kit
    GateMostly irrelevant on one-shot drums, and the reason to leave it at 100 there
    06Melodies — Range and Leap

    On a synth, MIDI or CV clip, turn Range up and the notes spread across rows above the one you picked. 7 is about an octave of an ordinary seven-note scale and is the place to start.

    Every note is in the song's key by construction rather than by correction — the line walks in scale degrees and those are turned into pitches afterwards, so it cannot land out of scale. Change the song's scale later and generate again, and the line follows.

    LeapWhat the line does
    0Only ever steps to the next note of the scale. A scale run, up and down
    20–40Mostly steps, with the occasional jump. This is where tunes live
    70–100Jumps constantly. Scattered, arpeggio-ish, harder to sing

    The line always starts on the row you picked, so that row is the tonic of what you get. It turns back when it reaches either end of the range rather than piling up against it, which is what a melody does and what stops the top note repeating.

    A wide Range and a long Gate is a different instrument

    At Gate above 100% a note runs past its step. Two notes in the same row are never allowed to overlap — the second one cuts the first short — but notes in different rows overlap freely, so a wide line with a long gate comes out as overlapping held notes rather than as a sequence of separate ones. On a pad or a string sound that is the interesting setting.

    If the row you picked is not in the song's key — an out-of-scale row, or a clip with no scale — the line falls back to chromatic degrees rather than refusing to write. An octave of semitones is a strange melody, but it is a melody, and going silent would just look broken.

    07It replaces, and undo is the way back

    Generating twice does not layer the second part over the first. The rows the line uses are cleared before it writes, so the Seed number always means what it says — otherwise walking through seeds would silt the clip up with every part you rejected.

    ActionWhat it affects
    Generate nowThe target row, and — at Range above 0 — the rows the line reaches. Rows outside that span are left alone
    UNDOOne whole generation, every row of it, in one press. A second undo takes back the one before that
    Rows it createdUndone with the notes — a row that did not exist before the generation does not survive undoing it
    Press undo from clip view, not from inside the menu

    Back out of the menu first. This is true of edits made from any menu, not just this one.

    What it writes is real notes and nothing about them is special: nudge them, re-length them, change velocities, delete half of them, or run Spice, Strum and Harmonize over the result. Generate is a starting point rather than a mode you are stuck in.

    08Known limits
    LimitWhat happens
    Rhythm only on a KitRange is ignored there by design — see section 05
    One row at a timeThere is no generate-the-whole-kit gesture. Each drum is its own press
    Monophonic linesOne note per step. It writes melodies, not chords
    No velocity or gate variationEvery generated note takes the row's default velocity and the same gate. Spice is how you thin and vary the result afterwards
    Clip view onlyThe target row comes from the clip view's idea of what you last touched, so the command is not available from Song view or the arranger
    Not automatableThe five controls are settings rather than parameters, so none has a CC or an automation lane. Generating is an edit, not something to sequence

    The five settings are saved with the song, so a pattern can be regenerated or adjusted later.

    No switch

    Generate has no switch of its own. It is part of SETTINGS → COMMUNITY FEATURES → Rudement upgrades → MIDI FX (MIFX, On by default), and it only writes when you press Generate now.

    ↑ Back to contents
    14Groove
    Synthstrom Deluge · Rudement Firmware
    Chapter 14

    Groove

    Swing, shuffle and feel templates for any clip, including Ableton grooves from the card

    Inspired by the OXI One's Groove and Ableton Live's Groove Pool, Groove plays a clip through a feel template: each step can land a little early or late and a little louder or softer. The notes on the grid never move. Turn Reset to Default and the clip plays exactly as you wrote it. Fourteen templates are built in, and Ableton .agr groove files load straight off the SD card. On a Kit it works per drum, or across the whole kit with Affect Entire.

    GROV · SETTINGS → COMMUNITY FEATURES → Rudement upgrades → Groove · Off by default · then SELECT → MIDI FX → Groove

    Your first minute

    #Do thisAnd watch
    1Turn on SETTINGS → COMMUNITY FEATURES → Rudement upgrades → GrooveOff by default
    2Play a clip of straight 16ths and open MIDI FX → GrooveTemplate Off, everything at 0
    3Turn Template to Swing 60Time jumps to 100 and Accent to 50. The off-beats swing and the downbeats lift
    4Turn Time up, then below 0Harder swing; below 0 the off-beats come early
    5Turn Reset to DefaultStraight again, exactly as written
    01The controls

    Six controls over two screens of the page; scroll right past Time for Random, Offset and Reset. Nothing is written into the clip, so every setting is non‑destructive and saves with the song.

    Control7SEGRangeDefaultWhat it does
    TemplateTMPLOff, 14 built‑ins, then the files in GROOVESOffThe feel: a timing and velocity offset for every step
    AccentACNT−120 to +120%0How much of the template's loud‑and‑soft shape you hear. Negative turns it upside down
    TimeTIME−120 to +120%0How much of the template's early‑and‑late shape you hear. Negative pushes late steps early
    RandomRAND0–100%0Loosens timing and velocity on every step, on top of the template. Works on its own too
    OffsetOFST0–63 steps0Slides the template along the beat, so its push lands on different steps
    ResetRSETDefault / Edited—Turn to Default to put every control back and play the clip straight. Reads Edited while anything is changed
    Picking a template fills in the amounts

    If Accent and Time are both at 0 when you choose a template, they are set for you so you hear it straight away: Time 100 and Accent 50 for a built‑in, or the amounts the groove was saved with for an Ableton file. Once you have set either one yourself, changing template leaves your amounts alone.

    02The built‑in templates
    TemplateStepsFeel
    Swing 54, 57, 60, 63, 6616thsClassic 16th swing, from barely there to almost triplet. The number is the swing percentage; 50 would be straight
    8th Swing 588thsSwing on the 8th notes rather than the 16ths
    Shuffle8thsA full triplet shuffle
    Laid Back16thsBackbeats and in‑between notes drag behind the beat
    Push16thsEverything but the downbeats rushes ahead
    Humanize2 barsSmall, uneven timing and level changes, like a player
    Drunk16thsLoose and late, with a dragging snare
    Downbeat Acc16thsAccents only: loud on the beat, quiet in between. No timing change
    Offbeat Acc16thsAccents only, on the off‑beat 8ths
    Hat Dynamics16thsA hi‑hat player's loud‑soft pattern with a touch of swing
    03Ableton grooves

    Make a folder called GROOVES in the root of the SD card and copy .agr files into it. They appear in the Template list after the built‑ins, named after the file. To get one from Live, save a groove from the Groove Pool, or use Extract Groove on any clip and save that.

    When you choose a groove file, Groove reads its timing, its velocities and its Timing, Velocity and Random amounts. A groove used in a song is saved inside the song, so the song still plays the same on a card without the file. A groove like that shows at the end of the Template list.

    "Can't read that groove file"

    Some older groove files are stored compressed and will not load. Open the groove in a current version of Live and save it again.

    04On a Kit, and with other effects

    On a Kit each drum has its own groove: select a drum to groove that drum, or hold AFFECT ENTIRE to set every drum at once. Swinging the hats while the kick stays straight is the usual move. With no drum selected and AFFECT ENTIRE off, the page hides. On a melodic clip the groove belongs to the clip, and every note of a chord moves together.

    A template shorter than the clip runs on across loops. A 16‑step groove on a 12‑step clip lands differently each time round, the same as on the OXI One. Groove works with the other MIDI FX pages, Play FX and Loop Remix, and a change made while SHIFT is held under Temp Hold is put back on release.

    05Known limits

    The first step of the loop always stays on the grid. Timing moves in sequencer ticks, about 10 ms at 120 BPM, so very fine grooves come out slightly coarser than in Live. Up to 64 files are listed, up to 32 different groove files can be in use at once, and long names are cut to 23 characters. The settings are not automatable and have no CC. Recording the clip onto another track records the written pattern, not the groove.

    Switching it off entirely

    SETTINGS → COMMUNITY FEATURES → Rudement upgrades → Groove (GROV), Off by default. Off: every clip plays exactly as written. A song saved with grooves keeps them and gets them back when you turn it On.
