    15Temp Hold
    Synthstrom Deluge · Rudement Firmware
    Chapter 15

    Temp Hold

    A change you are only trying out

    Hold SHIFT, change things, and let go: everything you touched goes back to where it was. A way to try a change in the middle of a take without having to remember where you started.

    HOLD · SHIFT + change · SETTINGS → COMMUNITY FEATURES → Rudement upgrades → Temp Hold · Off by default

    Your first minute

    #Do thisAnd watch
    1Turn on SETTINGS → COMMUNITY FEATURES → Rudement upgrades → Temp HoldOff by default
    2Hold SHIFT and turn a gold knob, for example the filterThe sound changes as usual
    3Let go of SHIFTThe filter jumps back to exactly where it was
    4Turn the same knob without SHIFTAn ordinary, permanent change
    01What it is

    Every knob on the Deluge commits. Turn the filter to hear where it goes and the filter is now there; getting back means remembering where it was and turning it back, which in the middle of a take is not a thing anyone does accurately.

    Temp Hold is the Torso T-1's Temp button. While SHIFT is down, the firmware writes down what each thing was the first time you touch it, and puts every one of them back when SHIFT comes up. Nothing is recorded, nothing is saved, and the return is exact rather than approximate.

    02The gesture

    Switch it on at SETTINGS → COMMUNITY FEATURES → Rudement upgrades → Temp Hold. It ships Off, and deliberately: SHIFT is held constantly for other reasons, and turning every held SHIFT into a hold that reverts would change the instrument under someone who never asked for it.

    GestureWhat happens
    Hold SHIFT, change things, releaseMomentary. Everything returns when SHIFT comes up
    Short-press SHIFT, change things, short-press againLatched, with Shift Is Sticky on. Both hands stay free in between
    A footswitch on the Temp Hold MIDI commandSame as holding SHIFT, but without the SHIFT modifier — see section 03
    SHIFT held with nothing touchedNothing. A hold costs nothing until something is changed

    The latched form works because Shift Is Sticky keeps SHIFT down after a short press, and Temp Hold ends when SHIFT is released, however that happens.

    Temp Hold Tails

    SETTINGS → COMMUNITY FEATURES → Rudement upgrades → Temp Hold Tails (TAIL) appears once Temp Hold is On, and is On by default. If you turn a delay up during a hold, its repeats ring out naturally when the hold ends instead of stopping dead. It changes nothing unless a hold touched a delay. Turn it Off if you want the delay cut the moment you let go.

    03A footswitch, and why it is not just SHIFT

    SETTINGS → MIDI → COMMANDS → Temp Hold learns whatever you send it — a note, a CC, or a program change, from whichever device sent it. Like every command in that list it is unassigned until you learn it, and the assignment lives in the unit's settings rather than in the song. Press engages the hold, release puts everything back.

    This is the form that matters live, because it is the only one that leaves both hands on the controls.

    Why not just learn a switch to the SHIFT command

    You can, and it works — SETTINGS → MIDI → COMMANDS → Shift drives the same button Temp Hold watches, so a switch learned there holds and releases exactly as the panel button does. The catch is that it engages all of SHIFT: with your foot down, every pad and button on the panel does its shifted job instead of its ordinary one. That is a trap in performance. The Temp Hold command engages the hold and nothing else, so the rest of the panel keeps behaving normally while you are holding.

    Either half holds, and the hold ends when both are clear. Releasing SHIFT with your foot still down leaves everything where it is, and so does lifting your foot while SHIFT is held. Without that rule the two halves fight, and whichever you let go of first wins.

    04What it reaches

    Temp Hold covers the controls people actually perform with:

    HeldDetail
    Gold-knob paramsWhatever the knobs currently address — in a clip, in song mode, in the arranger, in automation view
    MIDI FXVelocity, Gate, Repeat, Delay, Spice and Dice, Strum, Loop Remix and Groove
    Spice & DiceBoth, so a variation can be auditioned and dropped
    Play FXClock Shift, Beat Stretch and Division

    It works the same everywhere the gold knobs work: in a clip it holds the clip's values, in Song view it holds the song's.

    On a Kit, MIDI FX and Play FX follow the rule the rest of that page group follows: one drum, or every drum under AFFECT ENTIRE. A hold taken with AFFECT ENTIRE down restores the whole kit.

    What it does not reach

    Values changed in the sound menus are not held, so Bouls, Wisps, Gristleator, Sear and the EQ are held only where their params sit under a gold knob, not when you edit them in a menu. Spread, Stochastic, Harmonize and Generate are not held either. Kit Split, Scene Capture and Grid Column Reorder are actions rather than values, so there is nothing to put back. Tempo and transport are deliberately outside it, as they are on the T-1.

    05Automation is off while it is held

    A change made during a hold is a live value change only. It never writes into an automation lane.

    Without it a temp twist would carve a real automation curve into the clip, and the restore would carve a second one over the top — the exact opposite of a change that leaves nothing behind.

    The cost of the guarantee

    You cannot record automation while SHIFT is held. If you are writing a curve, let go of SHIFT first. Everything else about the knob behaves normally.

    06Known limits
    LimitWhat happens
    Menu values outside MIDI FXNot held
    16 parameters and 48 MIDI FX settings per holdPast that the extra changes are let through unheld rather than dropped, and Too many changes to undo / FULL appears once
    A hold that spans a song loadRestores nothing. What it was holding belongs to a project that is no longer loaded

    When the hold is full, your change is still made; it just will not be put back on release.

    Switching it off entirely

    SETTINGS → COMMUNITY FEATURES → Rudement upgrades → Temp Hold (HOLD), Off by default. Off: SHIFT behaves exactly as stock. Temp Hold Tails (TAIL) appears once Temp Hold is On.

    16Morph
    Synthstrom Deluge · Rudement Firmware
    Chapter 16

    Morph

    Sixteen saved states of the whole song, and a knob that travels between any two

    Get the song sounding the way you want the verse. Press a knob: that is slot 1. Change whatever you like — a filter, a drum's saturation, the reverb, four things at once — and press again: that is slot 2, and one knob now travels between the two, moving everything you touched together. Keep going and the bank fills up to sixteen. Turn the other knob to any slot, press it, and the first knob takes you from where you are to there. All of it saves with the song.

    MRPH · MSLT · Envelope mod button · nothing to switch on

    Your first minute

    #Do thisAnd watch
    1In Song view, press the Envelope mod buttonThe gold knobs are now Morph: the upper one sweeps, the lower one picks a slot
    2Press the upper knobSLOT 1: the song as it sounds now
    3Change a filter and the reverb, then press the upper knob again1 TO 2 and a count of what moved: slot 2 is captured, knob at 50
    4Turn the upper knob down to 0 and backEverything you changed moves together between the two slots
    5Send CC 102 from a controllerThe same sweep, from the controller (section 09)
    01What it is

    A crossfader between states of the entire song — every parameter on every synth, kit row, audio clip and the song's own master chain. You capture states into a bank of sixteen numbered slots, and sweep between any two of them.

    It never stores a state to play back. It stores the difference. Two states of a song are thousands of numbers each and almost all of them are identical; the few that are not are the ones you changed. Morph keeps only those, so the work it does while you sweep is proportional to what you touched, not to how big the song is.

    The consequence, stated plainly

    Only what differs between the two slots moves. If you want the knob to reach something, change it between captures. Something you set once and never touched again is the same in every slot, so there is nothing for the knob to do to it.

    02The two knobs

    In Song view, press the Envelope mod button so the gold knobs are on that pair. Stock firmware gives a song nothing on these two knobs, so Morph displaces nothing.

    GestureWhat it does
    Upper knob — pressCapture the song into the next empty slot. The knob then sweeps from the slot you were on to the new one.
    Upper knob — turnSweep between the two slots. At 0 and at 50 the screen names the slot you have arrived at.
    Lower knob — turnSelect a slot, one slot per click.
    Lower knob — pressCue the selected slot. The upper knob now runs from where you are to that slot.
    SHIFT + lower knob — pressReplace the selected slot with the song as it sounds right now.

    There is nothing to switch on: with no captures taken the knobs have nothing to do, which is the off state.

    03Capturing

    The first press fills slot 1 and says SLOT 1. There is nothing to sweep yet. Change something and press again: the screen says 1 TO 2 moved 3 — you are now on slot 2, the knob sweeps between 1 and 2, and three things differ between them.

    After a capture the upper knob sits at 50, because the new slot is what you are already hearing. Turning it down toward 0 takes you back to the slot you came from.

    Captures always go into the next empty slot and never overwrite. When all sixteen are full the screen says BANK FULL and nothing is captured — use replace (section 05) to reuse a slot.

    Change something, then capture

    If nothing has changed since the slot you are on, the press says NO CHANGE from slot n and does not spend a slot. Mid-sweep you are hearing a blend of two slots rather than a state you chose, so if you want to keep going from there, tweak something first.

    04Going back to a slot

    Turn the lower knob. Each click moves one slot and the screen says SLOT 7, or SLOT 7 empty if nothing has been captured there.

    Press the lower knob to cue it. The screen says 2 TO 7 moved 5: the upper knob now runs from the slot you were on (2) to the one you cued (7). Nothing changes when you press. The upper knob is parked at 0 — where you already are — and turning it up walks the song into slot 7.

    The 0 end is the song as it sounds at the moment you cue, including anything you tweaked since slot 2. The screen calls it by the slot you were last on, because that is the useful name for it.

    Cueing an empty slot says SLOT 7 empty and changes nothing.

    05Replacing a slot

    Select a slot with the lower knob, get the song sounding the way you want that slot to sound, then hold SHIFT and press the lower knob. The screen says 2 TO 5 REPLACED moved 3. Only that slot changes; the other fifteen are untouched. This is also the way out of BANK FULL.

    Replacing the slot you are already on gives you a sweep from its old version to its new one, labelled OLD 2 TO 2, and the knob at 0 shows OLD SLOT 2. The old version is gone as soon as you capture or cue something else.

    Why SHIFT + press does not delete automation here

    On every other gold knob, SHIFT + press deletes that knob's automation. On the slot knob it replaces the slot instead — the slot selector has nothing worth automating, and the gesture was worth more here.

    06What the screen says

    Every press answers with a message that holds for about three seconds. Numbers are slot numbers, except after moved, which counts how many things differ between the two ends.

    MessageWhat happened
    SLOT 1First capture. Nothing to sweep yet.
    1 TO 2 moved 3Captured slot 2. The upper knob sweeps from slot 1 (0) to slot 2 (50).
    2 TO 7 moved 5Cued slot 7 from slot 2. Knob at 0; turn up to go to 7.
    2 TO 5 REPLACED moved 3Slot 5 now holds the song as it sounds.
    OLD 2 TO 2 REPLACEDYou replaced the slot you were on; the sweep is old version to new.
    … no changeThe two ends are identical, so the knob has nothing to move.
    NO CHANGE from slot nNothing changed since slot n; no slot was used.
    SLOT n at 0 or 50The upper knob has arrived at an end: you are hearing slot n.
    BANK FULLAll sixteen slots are used. Replace one (section 05).
    BANK RESET song changedA clip, kit row or drum was added or removed. The slots describe a song shaped differently, so they are cleared rather than applied to the wrong parameters.
    TOO MANY moved nThe two states differ in too many places to morph — that is a different song, not a tweak.
    07What travels, and what does not

    Everything that differs arrives at the same time. A parameter that moves a long way and one that barely moves both complete their journey across the same knob travel.

    Reached: synth and drum parameters, kit rows drum by drum, audio clip parameters, existing non-automated MIDI CC values, the song's master chain, and saturation.

    For a MIDI clip, Morph records the current value of every CC already present in that clip. Moving Morph interpolates and transmits those CC values to the external instrument. A CC with automation remains under its automation and is skipped.

    Not reached:

    • Anything automated. It rewrites itself from its automation every tick, so a morph write would be overwritten; it is skipped rather than fought.
    • CV clips. They have no parameter collection equivalent to MIDI CC values to sweep.
    • Notes, clips, arrangement, anything structural. Morph moves sound, not music.
    08Saving with the song

    Save the song and the whole bank goes with it: every captured slot, which slot the lower knob points at, and which two slots the upper knob is set between. Load it again and the knob is still between the same two slots at the same position. Nothing jumps; the next turn carries on from where you left it.

    Two things do not come back exactly:

    • After a cue, the 0 end reloads as the slot you cued from. Tweaks you had made on top of that slot before cueing are not kept.
    • An OLD end (section 05) is not saved; the pair is dropped and the slots are kept.
    When a saved bank is dropped on load

    If the song's parameter layout changes, Morph clears its bank and shows BANK RESET song changed instead of applying values to the wrong targets. The song itself still loads normally.

    09Over MIDI

    The upper knob's position is a song parameter, so it can be automated on the song's lane and has a MIDI Follow controller. The slot selector is also a song parameter and saves with the song, but has no default controller.

    WhatValueNotes
    Upper knob (sweep)CC 102MIDI Follow default. Sweeps Morph in Song, Arranger and Performance views, whichever track is selected. Inside a clip, CC 102 goes to that clip instead (Env 3 attack on a synth). Set Takeover to Jump for an absolute fader.
    CaptureMIDI commandSETTINGS → MIDI → COMMANDS → Morph Capture. Learn it to a footswitch.
    Slot select, cue, replace—On the lower knob only.
    10If it seems not to be working
    What you seeWhy
    The upper knob does nothingOnly one slot captured, or the last message ended in no change. It takes two different states.
    moved 2 after changing three thingsOne of the three is automated, on a CV clip, or not a parameter Morph reaches. Section 07.
    The knob stopped working after an editA clip, kit row or drum was added or removed. The next capture says BANK RESET song changed and starts a new bank.
    Automation deleted on SHIFT + pressYou pressed the upper knob. Replace is SHIFT + the lower knob.
    Pressing a knob shows a numberYou are not on the Envelope mod button, or not in Song view.
    Slots missing after loadingThe song loaded with a different parameter count than it was saved with. Section 08.
    No switch

    Morph has no switch. With no slots captured the two knobs have nothing to do, which is its off state.

    17Loop Remix
    Synthstrom Deluge · Rudement Firmware
    Chapter 17

    Loop Remix

    Rearrange a looping pattern in real time, without rewriting it

    Inspired by the Yamaha RS7000's Real Time Loop Remix, Loop Remix plays a clip back out of order while the written pattern stays exactly as you drew it. You choose how much of the loop moves and which arrangement it takes, press to apply, and the part reshuffles live. Turn Reset to Default and the clip is your pattern again, untouched. On a Kit it works per drum, or across the whole kit with Affect Entire.

    LRMX · SETTINGS → COMMUNITY FEATURES → Rudement upgrades → Loop Remix · Off by default · then SELECT → MIDI FX → Loop Remix

    Your first minute

    #Do thisAnd watch
    1Turn on SETTINGS → COMMUNITY FEATURES → Rudement upgrades → Loop RemixOff by default
    2On a looping clip, open MIDI FX → Loop RemixType 1, Variation Normal 1
    3Press SELECT on RemixThe clip plays back rearranged. The grid does not change
    4Change Variation and press Remix againA different arrangement
    5Turn Reset to DefaultYour pattern, exactly as written
    01The controls

    Remix, three settings, and Reset. Nothing is written into the clip, so every setting is non‑destructive and saves with the song. The Interval parameter and the Fill family are kept from later Yamaha hardware, beyond the original RS7000 set.

    Control7SEGRangeDefaultWhat it does
    RemixRMXpress SELECT—Applies the current settings. Press again after changing them to apply the new ones
    TypeTYPE1–161How much of the loop is rearranged, and how far from the original
    VariationVARfamily + indexNormal 1Which arrangement — Normal, Reverse, Break, Pitch, Roll, then Fill
    IntervalINT1–81The grid the rearrangement snaps to
    ResetRSETDefault / Edited—Turn to Default to stop the remix and return the plain pattern. Reads Edited while anything is changed, like every other Reset in MIDI FX
    Nothing changes on screen

    The clip still holds the notes you wrote, so the only confirmation is what you hear — the same as Spice, Play FX and Strum. Variation reads as a family and an index (Normal 1–16, then Reverse, Break, Pitch, Roll, then Fill 1–48) rather than a bare 1–128 number.

    02Using it live

    Set Type, Variation and Interval, then press SELECT on Remix to hear the rearrangement. Change any setting and press again to move to it. For variations you want to keep, copy the clip down its column — the remix saves with the song, so a row of copies is a row of live variations you can launch. The rearrangement is musically beat‑aligned: it keeps every hit on the grid and the downbeat anchored at the lower Types, so it reshuffles rather than scrambles.

    03On a Kit, and with other effects

    On a Kit each drum has its own remix: select a drum to remix that drum, or hold AFFECT ENTIRE to set every drum at once. With no drum selected and AFFECT ENTIRE off, the page hides. On a melodic clip the remix belongs to the clip.

    Loop Remix changes where the clip is read, so it works with the other MIDI FX pages exactly as Play FX does. A change made while SHIFT is held under Temp Hold is put back on release.

    04Known limits

    Nothing on screen shows the remix; judge it by ear. The settings are not automatable and have no CC. Recording the clip onto another track records the written pattern, not the remix.

    Switching it off entirely

    SETTINGS → COMMUNITY FEATURES → Rudement upgrades → Loop Remix (LRMX), Off by default. Off: every clip plays exactly as written. A song saved with a remix keeps its settings and gets them back when you turn it On.

    18Scene Capture
    Synthstrom Deluge · Rudement Firmware
    Chapter 18

    Scene Capture

    Operating manual for keeping the combination you just found

    In Grid view you audition a combination by hand — kick from row 1, snare from row 3, hats stopped — and then have no way to keep it. Scene Capture is SAVE plus any section pad: it copies everything that is sounding into the first unused row below the populated ones, and that row's own section pad brings the combination back later.

    Community Features · Scene Capture

    Your first minute

    #Do thisAnd watch
    1Turn on SETTINGS → COMMUNITY FEATURES → Rudement upgrades → Scene CaptureOff by default
    2In Song view, get a combination playing: some clips running, some stoppedThis is what will be captured
    3Hold SAVE and press any section padA new, muted row appears below the populated rows, holding a copy of every clip you can hear. Playback carries on
    4Press the new row's section padEverything outside the row stops and the row starts, on the launch grid
    5Stop everything and try the gesture againNONE: nothing was sounding, so nothing is captured
    01The gesture

    Hold SAVE, press any section pad. The pad you press does not choose where the row lands — the row always goes below the lowest populated one, so the grid grows downward and nothing you have already built moves.

    The new row arrives muted, and the clips that were playing carry on playing. Capturing never interrupts what you are listening to, which is the whole point of being able to do it mid-performance.

    Two things stop it: there is no free row left, or nothing is sounding. Both say so on the display — FULL and NONE — and change nothing.

    02What gets captured

    The test is audibility, not what happens to be loaded in a column. A track that is stopped, muted, or silenced by another track's solo leaves its column blank in the captured row.

    These are copies, not references. Editing a source clip afterwards does not change the captured one, and each capture costs RAM. That is a deliberate trade: a row of real clips inherits every behaviour the firmware already has for clips, and a row of references would have had to reimplement all of it.

    03Bringing it back

    Press the captured row's section pad. Everything outside the row stops, everything in it starts, quantised to the launch grid — or immediately, with SHIFT.

    The row is an ordinary section holding ordinary clips, so it survives a save and reload untouched, and you can rename, edit or delete its clips like any others.

    04Limits worth knowing

    The row count is the ceiling. A song has 24 rows available. Captures use free rows; when none remain, the display shows FULL.

    It is a snapshot, not a link. Ableton calls the equivalent "Capture and Insert Scene", and this is that, minus the live link.

    RAM per capture. Every captured clip is a real clip. On a large song, many captures add up.

    Switching it off entirely

    SETTINGS → COMMUNITY FEATURES → Rudement upgrades → Scene Capture (CAPT), Off by default. Off turns the SAVE + section pad gesture off. Rows you have already captured stay in the song as ordinary rows.

    ↑ Back to contents
    19MIDI Follow: Grid Hold-to-Lock
    Synthstrom Deluge · Rudement Firmware
    Chapter 19

    MIDI Follow: Grid Hold-to-Lock

    A brief hold on a grid pad claims it as the MIDI Follow target

    In Grid view's Launch (green) mode, a brief hold locks MIDI Follow to a clip. Notes, pitch bend, aftertouch, modulation, MPE and CCs follow that lock with the pulse. Quick launch taps keep their normal behaviour without changing the lock. Scrolling the clip offscreen hides its pulse without moving the target.

    LOCK · SETTINGS → COMMUNITY FEATURES → Rudement upgrades → Grid Follow Lock · Off by default · Hold Time · Grid view, Launch mode
    01What it is

    The conflict happens because Grid view normally makes the last clip you touch the target for MIDI Follow. That is useful until you tap another clip merely to launch it: MIDI Follow then leaves the instrument you were editing and follows the clip you just launched. Hold-to-Lock solves the conflict where it occurs, on the grid. A pad tap still launches or stops the clip. A brief pad hold — past SETTINGS → DEFAULTS → Hold Time, then released within two seconds — makes that clip the persistent target for MIDI Follow's A/B/C channels. It uses the same Hold Time threshold as the existing SHIFT hold gesture.

    The two-second ceiling is there because holding a pad is also how you read a track's name on the display. Keep a pad down past two seconds and the lock is left exactly as it was, claimed or clear.

    tap → launch / stop the clip, as always (under Hold Time – 100 ms by default) hold → lock MIDI Follow onto this clip (past Hold Time, released inside 2 sec) "Follow: <track name>" confirms it on screen keep holding → nothing. Read the track name off the display; the lock stays where it was (past 2 sec) hold the SAME pad again → unlock ("Follow: unlocked") hold a DIFFERENT pad → move the lock there instead

    Once locked, the target sticks through anything else you tap on the grid — launching other clips, stopping them, arming them — none of that touches the lock. The lock moves when you let go, not while the pad is down: a knob turned mid-hold still reaches whatever was locked before, so the target and the pulse always agree. It works in Launch (green) mode only; Edit (blue) mode is untouched.

    02Using it

    Your first minute

    #Do thisAnd watch
    1Turn on SETTINGS → COMMUNITY FEATURES → Rudement upgrades → Grid Follow Lock (LOCK)Nothing changes yet; it only enables the hold gesture below
    2Recommended: set SETTINGS → DEFAULTS → Hold Time to 500 MSA launch tap can no longer lock by accident. Only a deliberate half-second hold does
    3Set a MIDI Follow channel (A, B, or C) to a controller channel, as usualFollow behaves exactly as before — this chapter only changes how its target gets picked in Grid view
    4In Grid view, Launch (green) mode, hold a pad past Hold Time and let go within two secondsA popup reads Follow: <track name>, and the grid's selection pulse settles on that pad
    5Let go, then tap a few other pads to launch clipsClips launch normally; the pulse stays on the locked pad throughout, and so does Follow's target
    6Turn a knob mapped to FollowIt controls the locked clip, not whatever was last tapped
    7Hold any pad down and keep holding — past two secondsIts track name is on the display to read; no popup, and the lock has not moved
    8Hold the locked pad again, brieflyA popup reads Follow: unlocked; the pulse returns to following ordinary selection

    A knob turned during a hold still reaches whatever was locked before (or the ordinary target, if nothing is locked). The new lock takes over when you let go, at the same moment the pulse moves, so the pad that pulses is always the clip the knobs control.

    Off by default

    Grid Hold-to-Lock is switched on at SETTINGS → COMMUNITY FEATURES → Rudement upgrades → Grid Follow Lock (LOCK). It ships Off because Hold Time is only 100 ms: a slightly slow launch tap is enough to lock, and from then on your controller ignores the clip on screen. If MIDI Follow seems stuck on one track, that is what happened — hold the pulsing pad briefly to unlock it, or turn the switch Off.

    Suggested setting: Hold Time 500 ms. When you use the lock, set SETTINGS → DEFAULTS → Hold Time to 500 MS. At 100 ms a launch tap that lingers a little turns into a lock. At 500 ms only a deliberate half-second hold locks, and you still have a 0.5 to 2 second window to let go in. Hold Time is a global setting, so it also changes how long SHIFT, button holds and Performance View's FX pad latch take to count as a hold.

    With the switch Off, MIDI Follow works as in the stock firmware: the pad you are holding, otherwise the clip on screen. Turning the switch Off also releases any lock that is standing. If every MIDI Follow channel is Off, the gesture has no effect either way.

    ↑ Back to contents
    20OLED Visualizer (Bonus)
    Synthstrom Deluge · Rudement Firmware
    Chapter 20

    OLED Visualizer (Bonus)

    Bonus feature: eleven views of audio and MIDI on the OLED

    The Visualizer was created by Bruce Zawadzki (Tone Coder / bzawad) and adapted for this firmware by Rudement. Watch the Deluge's audio output or MIDI notes in Song or Arranger view; the Visualizer changes the display only.

    VIS · VPRI · SHIFT + LEVEL · OLED only

    Your first minute

    #Do thisAnd watch
    1Open SETTINGS → COMMUNITY FEATURES → Rudement upgrades → Visualizer and choose WaveformOff by default. OLED only
    2In Song view, press SHIFT + LEVELVISUALIZER ON, and the OLED draws the output
    3Press KITLine Spectrum
    4Press CV a few timesSteps through the other eight displays
    5Press SHIFT + LEVEL againThe normal screen returns
    01Enable and show it
    1. Open SETTINGS → COMMUNITY FEATURES → Rudement upgrades → Visualizer (VIS) and choose a mode. The default is Off.
    2. Return to Song or Arranger view and press SHIFT + LEVEL, the first gold-knob mode button. The popup reads VISUALIZER ON.
    3. Press the same combination again to turn the display off. A selected mode also replaces the VU meter when the VU meter is shown.

    The saved Community Features choice is the starting mode. Button-selected modes are temporary overrides. The Visualizer is available on OLED displays; it does not appear in clip editing screens.

    02Choose a display

    With the Visualizer active in Song or Arranger view, release any held clip pad before using these buttons.

    ButtonMode
    SYNTHWaveform
    KITLine Spectrum
    MIDIPiano Roll
    CV, repeatedlyGraphic EQ, Stereo Spectrum, Stereo EQ, Cube, Skyline, Starfield, Tunnel, Pulse Grid, then back to Graphic EQ

    CV remembers the last mode used in its group. Graphic EQ is the Bar Spectrum display: a meter, with no effect on the sound. The two stereo modes show left and right channels separately.

    03Priority and temporary readouts

    Visualizer Priority (VPRI) is in the same Community Features group and defaults to Off. It is shown when a Visualizer mode is selected.

    PriorityWhat happens while the Visualizer is visible
    OffGold-knob values, manual tempo changes and other temporary messages take the screen, then the graph returns. A pending launch countdown can keep the screen until the launch completes.
    OnThe graph keeps the screen. Knob and tempo changes still take effect, but their readouts are suppressed while the Visualizer is displayed.

    When the Deluge follows an external clock, automatic tempo estimates do not open popups over an active Visualizer. Without the Visualizer, the normal tempo readout remains available.

    04Silence and visibility

    Audio modes hide after about one second without audio above the display's silence threshold, and return when audio resumes. They read audio rendered by the Deluge; sending MIDI to an external instrument alone does not supply an audio signal to them. Piano Roll follows MIDI note activity instead.

    Waveform keeps drawing through zero crossings and quiet passages.

    Switching it off entirely

    SETTINGS → COMMUNITY FEATURES → Rudement upgrades → Visualizer (VIS), Off by default. Off skips the audio capture entirely. Visualizer Priority (VPRI) appears once a mode is chosen.

    ↑ Back to contents
    21USB Audio (Bonus)
    Synthstrom Deluge · Rudement Firmware
    Chapter 21

    USB Audio (Bonus)

    Bonus feature: eight tracks into your computer, four channels back, over one USB cable

    USB Audio was created by sticknobills and adapted for this firmware by Rudement. Plug the Deluge into a computer and it shows up as an audio interface as well as a MIDI device. Send each track to its own channel and record them as separate tracks in your DAW, with no extra cables and no driver to install. Four channels come back the other way, so the computer can feed effects or recordings into the song.

    Track menu → USB Routing · USBSETTINGS → USB Audio · OLVL · RTN · RLVL · CMP

    Your first minute

    #Do thisAnd watch
    1Connect the Deluge's USB port to the computerA new audio device named Deluge appears with 8 inputs. On Windows it is listed as Microphone (Deluge)
    2In your DAW, pick the Deluge as the audio input and turn on inputs 1 and 2. Arm a stereo track on input 1/2The track's meter stays still: nothing is being sent yet
    3On the Deluge, open a synth clip, press SELECT and go to USB Routing → USB Pair 1-2. Turn it OnThe OLED shows USB Pair 1-2 On (1-2 on 7-segment)
    4Play the clipThe DAW track's meter moves at about the same level as the Deluge's own meter. The Deluge still plays through its outputs too
    5Record in the DAW, then play it backThe take sounds like the synth did on the Deluge, without the song's master effects
    01What the computer sees

    The Deluge is a standard (class-compliant) USB audio device, so Windows and macOS use it with their built-in drivers. It shares the cable with USB MIDI, which keeps working as before.

    DirectionChannelsWhat they carry
    Deluge → computer8Whatever tracks you send there, from each track's USB Routing menu. Silent until you send something
    Computer → Deluge4Audio from the computer, used by USB Return or by an audio track's input (section 05)

    Audio runs at 44.1 kHz, 16-bit, which is the most a USB connection of this speed can carry in both directions at once.

    One thing it rules out

    While the Deluge is connected to a computer as an audio device, it cannot also host a USB MIDI controller plugged into it. MIDI to and from the computer still works, and so do the 5-pin MIDI ports.

    02Sending a track to the computer

    Open a synth, kit or audio clip, press SELECT, and go to USB Routing (USB). Every item is an On/Off switch, and any number can be On at once.

    Item7SEGWhat it does
    USB Channel 1–81 … 8Sends the track to that one channel, mixed down to mono
    USB Pair 1-2 … 7-81-2 … 7-8Sends the track to that pair in stereo: left on the first channel, right on the second
    Main MixMAINOn by default. Off takes the track out of the Deluge's own outputs, so you hear it only through the computer
    • It belongs to the track, not the clip. Launch another clip on the same track and it keeps going to the same channels.
    • Tracks can share a channel. Send three tracks to USB Pair 7-8 and the computer gets the three mixed together there.
    • A kit goes as one, all its drums together. To record drums on separate channels, use Kit Split (chapter 11) to put them on their own tracks first.
    • It is saved with the song.
    • MIDI and CV tracks make no sound on the Deluge, so they have no USB Routing item.

    What is in the copy. Each track arrives with its own sound, effects, volume and pan, but before the song's master section: no master volume, master filter, master compressor or song reverb. That is what you want for mixing in a DAW, and it is why a recording can sound a little drier than the same song from the Deluge's outputs.

    03Out Level

    SETTINGS → USB Audio → Out Level (OLVL) sets the level of all eight outgoing channels together.

    ValueWhat you get
    40 (default)The same level as the Deluge's own outputs. A loud track stays clear of clipping
    0–39Quieter, 1.2 dB per step. 0 is silent
    41–50Up to 12 dB louder, for quiet patches

    Out Level only changes what goes to the computer. The Deluge's own outputs and headphones are not affected. It is a setting on the Deluge, kept when you load another song.

    If a take comes in distorted

    Lower Out Level a few steps, or turn the track's volume down. Because the copy is taken before the master compressor, a very loud patch can clip at USB even when the Deluge's own outputs sound clean.

    04Setting up the computer

    Windows. The Deluge appears as Microphone (Deluge) with 8 channels.

    1. Open Settings → System → Sound, choose Microphone (Deluge), and turn off Voice Clarity and any Audio enhancements. Left on, Windows treats the Deluge like a microphone and changes the level and sound before your DAW gets it.
    2. Many DAWs, Ableton Live among them, want an ASIO driver. The Deluge does not need one of its own: install the free FlexASIO driver and point it at the Deluge, as below. Then choose FlexASIO as the audio device in the DAW and turn on the input channels you need.

    FlexASIO reads a small text file named FlexASIO.toml in your user folder (C:\Users\you). This one takes the Deluge's eight channels in and plays out through your usual interface. Replace the output device name with yours, exactly as Windows shows it:

    backend = "Windows WASAPI" bufferSizeSamples = 256 [input] device = "Microphone (Deluge)" channels = 8 [output] device = "Speakers (Your Interface)" channels = 2

    macOS. The Deluge appears in Audio MIDI Setup with no driver needed. Choose it as the input in your DAW. To listen through a different interface at the same time, combine the two in an Aggregate Device in Audio MIDI Setup.

    Listening. Sound that goes into the computer and back out to your speakers arrives late. On a Windows test setup with Ableton Live and a 256-sample buffer it was about 52 ms behind — enough to feel when you play. For no delay at all, listen from the Deluge's own outputs or headphones while you play, and set the DAW tracks' monitoring to Off so you don't hear both.

    05Bringing audio back from the computer

    The computer can send four channels to the Deluge. There are two ways to use them.

    Into the song mix. Under SETTINGS → USB Audio:

    Item7SEGWhat it does
    USB ReturnRTNWhich returning pair is mixed into the song: Off, 1-2 or 3-4. It joins before the song's master effects, filter, volume and compressor, so it is treated like one of the Deluge's own tracks. Off by default
    Return LevelRLVLLevel of that pair, 0–50 in 1.2 dB steps. 0 is silent, 40 leaves it as it arrives (the default), 50 is 12 dB louder
    Delay CompensationCMP0–100 ms. Holds the Deluge's own tracks back by this much, so a track sent out to an effect in the computer and returned lands in time with everything else. Set it to the round-trip delay of your setup. 0 is off (the default)

    Into an audio track. On an audio track, open the input selector (where you choose LEFT, RIGHT or STEREO), choose USB, then press SELECT and pick a channel:

    ItemWhat it does
    USB Channel 1–4That channel as the track's input, in mono
    USB Pair 1-2, 3-4That pair as the track's input, in stereo

    The track then plays and records the computer's audio just like a line input, through its own filters, effects, volume and pan. A pair that an audio track is using is not also added to the song by USB Return, so you never hear it twice.

    Delay Compensation delays your playing too

    With CMP above 0, everything you play on the Deluge, line inputs included, comes out that much later. Set it back to 0 when you are not routing through the computer.

    06Known limits
    LimitWhat happens
    Master sectionTracks go to USB before the song's master effects and volume (section 02)
    Main Mix Off and reverbA track taken out of the main mix still sends its reverb to the Deluge's outputs, so you may hear its tail there
    KitsRouted as a whole, not per drum
    USB MIDI hostNo USB MIDI controller can be plugged into the Deluge while it is connected to a computer as an audio device
    ProcessingEach channel a track is sent to costs a little processing. On a busy song, routing several tracks costs about one and a half voices
    Computer clockReturning audio occasionally drops a single sample to stay in step with the computer. You will not hear it
    Windows still shows an old layoutIf the computer saw an earlier USB-audio firmware, remove the Deluge in Device Manager, then plug it in again
    No switch

    USB Audio has no switch. The Deluge always appears to the computer as an audio device, but nothing is sent until you turn on a USB channel for a track, and Main Mix starts On, so the Deluge sounds exactly as it did before. Out Level, USB Return, Return Level and Delay Compensation are kept on the Deluge, not in the song.

    ↑ Back to contents
    22CPU Load
    Synthstrom Deluge · Rudement Firmware
    Chapter 22

    CPU Load

    What each feature costs, on a scale of 1 to 10

    The Deluge has a fixed processing budget for every audio block. When a song exceeds it, the CPU indicator flashes and the audio may become crackly, choppy, or lose voices.

    1–10 · one number per feature · reference
    01What the numbers mean

    The core runs at 400 MHz and the audio runs at 44,100 samples a second, which leaves roughly nine thousand instructions per sample for the whole machine — every voice you are playing, every effect on every track, and the song chain, together.

    Two things follow, and they explain the whole table below.

    Per-note decisions are much cheaper than per-sample audio processing. Note effects usually add little load by themselves; extra generated or repeated notes can still cost CPU because they create more voices.

    What multiplies a cost matters more than the cost. An effect on the song chain runs once. An effect on a track runs once per track you put it on. An effect inside a synth voice runs once per voice, so the same knob that costs nothing on a single held note costs ten times that on a ten-note chord.

    And averages are not what break a machine — spikes are. A feature that is quiet most of the time but occasionally does a great deal of work inside one block will cut voices where a steadily expensive one plays on happily.

    RatingWhat it means in practice
    1Free. Either nothing of it runs while audio is playing, or it is decided once per note. Use it everywhere, on everything
    2–3Light. You would have to stack it across a lot of tracks before it showed at all
    4–5Moderate. One or two are comfortable. Keep an eye on it as polyphony climbs
    6–7Heavy. Budget for it, and expect to give something up elsewhere in the song
    8–9Very heavy. One instance can dominate the machine; under load, voices will start going
    10Extreme. Can miss the deadline on its own. Voices cut out and stay out until the transport is restarted
    02Every feature, rated
    FeatureCPUMultiplied byWhat to know
    Wisps — Spectral9one at a timeThe heaviest mode: DSP peak about 90 on the unit, against 45 for Granular. Its 4,096-point transforms are spread a slice at a time across renders, and it runs mono to fit
    Wisps — Stretch8one at a timeDSP peak about 80. See chapter 07 for the measurements
    Wisps — Oliverb8one at a timeDSP peak about 80, and the highest average of the six
    Wisps — Resonestor7one at a timeDSP peak about 60, steady
    Wisps — Delay6one at a timeDSP peak about 47 — barely above Granular
    Wisps — Granular6one at a timeThe cheapest mode, DSP peak about 45, and still a full effect. Only one Wisps can run, in any mode — two Granulars together already overload the unit
    Bouls — Speech, Modal, String, six-op FM9× voicesA complete oscillator per voice at the demanding end of the Bouls models. Cost multiplies with every note held
    Bouls — Virtual Analog, Waveshaping, Wavetable, Chiptune6× voicesThe cheap end of the same engine. The other models sit between these two rows
    Gristleator5× tracks with it onThe free-running LFO is light. Raising Blend adds the song-synchronised two-lane gate and its smoothed amplitude, filter, or Dirt movement. Taking On down skips the complete effect after its short fade.
    Sear — drive5× voicesTwo processing passes per sample, per active voice.
    MIDI FX — Repeat, MIDI Delay4× echoesThe arithmetic is free. What costs is the voices: every repeat or echo is a voice, as expensive as the note that spawned it. A four-echo delay on a big chord is the same load as playing that chord five times
    Four-Band EQ — the two bell bands3× tracks with a bell liftedGenuinely free while flat. The bass and treble shelves are stock, and are not counted here
    Sear — Tone2× voicesA couple of operations per sample
    Delay Filters2× tracks with delayTwo simple filters inside each delay's feedback path. Measured: three tracks with both filters at mid-travel added about 2 samples on average and 6 at peak. Bypassed completely when the switch is Off
    Reverb HPF / LPF1once per songTwo simple filters on the one shared reverb return. Measured: no change on average, about 2 samples at peak
    Morph2× parameters that differWorks only while the upper knob is moving. Measured: no change on average, about 4 samples at peak while sweeping 8 changed parameters
    OLED Visualizer — Waveform, Line Spectrum, Piano Roll1onceMeasured: no change with Waveform drawing
    OLED Visualizer — Stereo Spectrum and other CV modes3onceMeasured with Stereo Spectrum: no change on average, but about 7 more samples at peak and a deeper buffer draw. With the switch Off nothing is captured
    USB Audio2× USB channels a track is sent toAbout 0.2% of the processor for each channel a track is sent to. On a busy song, routing several tracks costs about one and a half voices. Nothing is sent until a track has a USB channel On
    Spice & Dice, Strum, Spread, Stochastic, Harmonize, Generate, Gate Time, Velocity, Play FX, Loop Remix, Groove1—All decided once per note, which is thousands of times cheaper than anything per sample. Turn them all on at once and nothing measurable happens to your headroom
    Kit Split, Scene Capture, Grid Column Reorder, Track Edit, Altered-Note Shading, Chroma, MIDI Follow, Temp Hold1—None of these exist while audio is rendering — they are gestures, edits and screens. Their cost is exactly zero

    The ratings are relative guides. Actual headroom depends on polyphony, the selected Bouls model, Wisps mode, and the rest of the song. Treat the CPU indicator and audible breakup as the final test.

    03Switching a feature off does not give the CPU back
    The thing most people get wrong

    Turning DUST, GRIS, SEAR or EQ4 off in Community Features takes their menus away. It does not stop the processing, and it will not buy you a single cycle.

    That is deliberate, and it is worth knowing why: a song you saved with an effect dialled in has to play back exactly the same afterwards, including after you have tidied your Community Features list. So those toggles hide the door, not the room. Chapter 01 says the same thing in the language of toggles; this is what it means for load.

    What does switch a stage off is its own control, and every one of these is checked afresh a few thousand times a second, so the saving is immediate:

    To actually stopDo this
    WispsSet Mode to OFF. The engine stops and hands its memory back — it is not merely muted
    GristleatorTake On down. It is a threshold, not a blend, and below it the whole effect is skipped
    Four-Band EQ bellsLeave a bell flat. A band at zero gain is not computed
    SearTake Sear (the drive) to its minimum. The stage is skipped

    The note-event features are different again: Strum, Harmonize and Temp Hold do honour their toggles. But since all three rate 1, switching them off is a matter of keeping the instrument's behaviour where you want it, never of load.

    04What a feature costs just by being installed

    Installed features take up firmware storage, but that costs no audio time. A parameter you have not automated is never looked at while a song plays, so a feature you do not use is not quietly taxing your voices — it is simply resident. There is nothing to switch off and nothing to worry about.

    The one trade worth knowing: while Wisps is actually running it holds about 180 KB of the same pool the Deluge uses to cache audio from the card, so a busy sample-heavy song has slightly less cached audio to work with. Switch its mode to OFF and that memory goes straight back.

    A Wisps keeps an idle track running

    A synth or kit row normally stops rendering once its last note has finished. With Wisps on and Blend above 0, it keeps rendering even with no notes playing, so that grains, repeats, tails and a frozen buffer can carry on sounding. That costs CPU on a track that sounds silent. On a track you are not using, set Blend to 0 or take Mode to OFF.

    05When you run out

    You will hear it rather than see it: notes stop starting, or a held sound goes silent, and it does not recover on its own. The engine drops voices to make the deadline and does not bring them back until the transport is stopped and started.

    Give things up in this order, because it follows the table:

     Try this firstWhy
    1Change Wisps to a cheaper mode, or take it to OFFWisps is the heaviest single effect here, so changing its mode is the biggest saving in one move. One instance at its defaults runs with no culls in any mode, so it usually becomes a problem only alongside other heavy features
    2Bring the polyphony down on a Bouls synth, or move it to a cheaper engineIts cost is per voice, so this is the one place where playing fewer notes is a real saving
    3Turn the Gristleator's On down, or flatten an EQ bell, on tracks that do not need itPer-track costs add up quietly across a full song
    4Reduce a MIDI FX Repeat or Delay countEvery echo is a whole voice

    Nothing sequencer-side ever needs to be part of that list. Spice, Dice, Strum, Harmonize, the gate and velocity pages, Temp Hold and every grid gesture can all stay exactly as you like them — they are not what ran you out of room.

    06Reading SETTINGS → CPU

    The ratings above are guides. SETTINGS → CPU shows what your song is actually costing, measured on your own Deluge. The page is read-only, with Reset counters at the bottom.

    A sample here is one 44.1 kHz sample's worth of time. The engine renders audio in windows of at most 128 samples, and it starts culling voices when one render costs more than 80.

    ReadingWhat it showsWhat to look for
    DSP samplesThe average cost of one render, in samplesThe headline number. At 20 about three quarters of the machine is spare; near 80 voices start being culled
    DSP peak samplesThe worst single render since the last resetSpikes. A high peak with a low average is a feature doing a burst of work now and then
    Load x10The audio engine's share of time since the reset, times ten873 means 87.3%. The overall answer to "how loaded is this song"
    Window samplesHow far the output buffer drained, on average, between rendersRises with load. This is what the engine uses to size its windows
    Window peakThe furthest the buffer drained since the reset128 means the buffer ran dry. The closer to 128, the less margin is left
    Direness / Direness peakHow hard pressed the engine is, 0 to 14, now and at its worst since the resetAbove 0, the engine has started making load decisions. A peak above 0 after a quiet passage means something spiked
    Voices nowVoices sounding at the moment the screen drewNot a peak. To find how many voices fit, play a set number and watch the culls
    Soft cullsVoices forced into an early releaseHeard as a part fading out early
    Hard cullsVoices cut off outrightHeard as a click or a note vanishing. Anything above 0 means the song is over budget
    RendersRenders counted since the resetA quick check that the page is live

    Every number runs from power-on or from the last reset, so an old peak can sit on the page long after the song that caused it. Always reset before you measure. Values can also lag by one render.

    The page cannot time one feature by itself. To find out what a feature costs, measure the same part twice:

    1. Set up the part with the feature off.
    2. Wait 2 seconds, then select Reset counters.
    3. Play for 30 seconds, then note DSP samples, DSP peak samples, Window peak and both cull counts.
    4. Turn the feature on and repeat steps 2 and 3.

    The difference between the two runs is what the feature costs. Chapter 07 lists these measurements for each Wisps mode.

    ↑ Back to contents
    23MIDI Implementation Chart
    Synthstrom Deluge · Rudement Firmware
    Chapter 23

    MIDI Implementation Chart

    Reference for default CC assignments and MIDI control

    Use this chapter to find each default MIDI CC, identify controls that require MIDI Learn, and avoid assignment conflicts.

    CC · FOLLOW · LEARN
    01How to read this chart

    Three separate things decide whether a MIDI CC reaches a control, and this chart tracks all three:

    Default CC (MIDI Follow). A fixed assignment works as soon as a MIDI Follow channel is configured. A hand-edited MIDI Follow settings file can override the defaults.

    Shortcut grid. A control with a fixed pad on the shortcut grid also appears in the Automation View parameter list.

    MIDI Learn. Hold LEARN and move a controller to assign that CC to the selected control in the song. Modulation-capable parameters support learning; menu selections and momentary actions do not.

    02The Gristleator — chapter 06
    Control7SEGDefault CC
    OnGON89
    RateGRAT114
    DepthGDEP115
    ShapeGSHP116
    BiasGBIA117
    ModeGMOD118
    FreqGFRQ119
    ResoGRES92
    LevelGLVL94
    DirtGDRT95
    PatternGPAT90
    VariationGVAR9
    SyncGSYN8
    BlendGBLD2
    03The Four-Band EQ — chapter 03

    All eight EQ controls have default CCs.

    Control7SEGDefault CC
    Bass amountBASS86
    Bass freqBAFR84
    Low mid amountLMID88
    Low mid freqLMFR33
    High mid amountHMID34
    High mid freqHMFR35
    Treble amountTREB87
    Treble freqTRFR85

    Bass and treble are included so the chart can be used to check CC collisions across the complete EQ.

    04Sear — chapter 05

    Sear drive is a patched parameter on default CC 22. STon is an unpatched modulation-capable parameter on default CC 31. MIDI Learn can assign either control.

    Control7SEGDefault CC
    Sear (drive)SEAR22
    Sear toneSTon31

    The stock Wavefolder is on CC 19, close to Sear drive on CC 22.

    05Bouls — chapter 02

    Harmonics, Timbre and Morph were never given CCs of their own — as chapter 02 explains, they reuse three parameter slots that already existed for other oscillator types, and inherit whatever CC already controlled that slot. There is nothing Bouls-specific to remap: point a controller at Oscillator 1's Pulse Width and Wave Index, or Oscillator 2's Pulse Width, and Bouls answers.

    Bouls controlBorrowed slotDefault CC
    HarmonicsOsc 1 Pulse Width23
    TimbreOsc 1 Wave Index25
    MorphOsc 2 Pulse Width28

    All three cover their full range from a controller: CC 0–127 sweeps the whole of each control, the same travel as 0–50 in the menu. Timbre's slot is centred, so CC 25 at 64 is Timbre at its middle.

    Model, Low-pass gate, LPG decay/colour and Aux output are menu selections, not modulatable parameters — no CC of any kind reaches them.

    06Wisps — chapter 07

    None of Wisps' nine continuous parameters has a shortcut-grid pad, so none has a default CC or appears in the Automation View parameter list — see chapter 07. Every one of them is still an ordinary automatable parameter underneath, so MIDI Learn works control by control, and a fixed CC can be hand-written into SETTINGS/MIDIFollow.XML for any of them; the tag is there with a value of 255 (unmapped) waiting to be edited.

    Control7SEGDefault CCMIDI Learn
    BlendBlnd—Yes
    PositionPosn—Yes
    SizeSize—Yes
    PitchPtch—Yes
    DensityDens—Yes
    TextureText—Yes
    SpreadSprd—Yes
    FeedbackFdbk—Yes
    ReverbVerb—Yes
    ModeDUST—No — not a parameter
    Freeze——No — not a parameter
    07Morph — chapter 16

    Morph's upper knob, the sweep between two slots, is a song parameter on default CC 102. It sweeps Morph in Song, Arranger and Performance views, whichever track is selected; inside a clip, CC 102 goes to that clip instead. MIDI Learn works too.

    The lower knob (slot select, cue and replace) has no CC. SETTINGS → MIDI → COMMANDS → Morph Capture is a global MIDI command that captures the next slot; like every command in that list it is unassigned until you learn it.

    Control7SEGDefault CC
    Morph (upper knob)MRPH102
    Morph slot (lower knob)MSLT—
    08Kit Split and Chroma — chapters 11 & 12

    Kit Split is a one-shot menu action, not a parameter of any kind — it has no CC, no shortcut-grid position, and nothing to MIDI-learn. Nothing about it belongs in a CC chart, and it is listed here only to say so explicitly.

    Chroma is a performance surface, not a bank of automatable parameters: the palette and iso grids pick and voice chords locally, and none of that is exposed as a modulation destination a MIDI CC could drive. The one place chapter 12 uses the word LEARN is the chord-bank sidebar (hold a sidebar column, turn the vertical encoder) — that binds a physical pad column to chord memory, and has nothing to do with incoming MIDI CCs. Neither feature appears in the reference table below.

    09MIDI FX and Spice & Dice — chapter 13, section 13.4

    None of the MIDI FX settings has a CC, default or learnable. They are per-clip and per-drum settings rather than modulation-capable parameters. MIDI clips do carry CC values for the external instrument, but those CCs do not address MIDI FX settings; CV clips have no comparable CC collection. Nothing about the MIDI FX settings belongs in a CC chart, and they are listed here to say so rather than to leave the absence unexplained.

    Dice is the exception, and it is not a CC mapping. SETTINGS → MIDI → COMMANDS → Dice is a global MIDI command, in the same list as the transport commands, and it learns whatever is sent to it — a note, a CC, or a program change, from whichever device sent it. There is no default: like every command in that list it is unassigned until you learn it, and the assignment lives in the unit's settings rather than in the song.

    It is momentary and song-wide — one press rolls a new variation for every clip and every drum that has Spice turned up, and nothing happens on the note-off. See section 13.4, part 06.

    10Temp Hold — chapter 15

    Temp Hold has no CC and nothing to MIDI-learn as a parameter: it is a gesture, not a value, and what it holds is whatever else you touch while it is engaged.

    It does have a command. SETTINGS → MIDI → COMMANDS → Temp Hold sits in the same list as the transport commands and learns whatever is sent to it — a note, a CC, or a program change, from whichever device sent it. No default, unassigned until learned, stored in the unit's settings rather than in the song. Unlike Dice it answers on both halves: press engages the hold, release puts every held value back.

    COMMANDS → Shift reaches the same feature, because it drives the button Temp Hold watches — but it brings the whole SHIFT modifier with it. Chapter 15, part 03, covers which of the two you want.

    11Harmonize — section 13.6

    Harmonize has no CC, no command, and nothing to MIDI-learn. Follow Chords and Chord Track are menu settings on the MIDI FX page group, like Spice and Dice before them — and unlike Dice, neither has been given a command, because neither is a thing you reach for mid-bar.

    What it does answer to indirectly is the chord track: launching a different clip on that track changes the progression every following clip is reading, so anything that can launch a clip — a program change, a MIDI Follow gesture, the grid — changes the harmony too.

    12Strum — section 13.2

    Strum has no CC, no command, and nothing to MIDI-learn. Time, Direction and Contour are menu settings on the MIDI FX page group, like Spice, Dice and the Harmonize pair before them — and like Harmonize, none of the three has been given a command either, because none is a thing you reach for mid-bar.

    The absence is worth stating rather than leaving to be discovered: it means a strum cannot be automated, swept from a controller, or recorded into an automation lane. That is the same trade every MIDI FX setting makes: the setting works identically on Synth, MIDI and CV clips, independently of the parameter collections each clip type provides.

    What Strum does change, from this chart's point of view, is when the notes it spreads leave the instrument — so a clip sending to external gear sends the chord spread across those ticks, not the block. Anything downstream counting on simultaneous note-ons will see the spread.

    13Generate, Spread and Stochastic — sections 13.7, 13.3 & 13.5

    None of the three has a default CC, and none can be MIDI-learned, for the reason section 09 gives for the rest of MIDI FX: they are settings rather than modulation-capable parameters, so they work consistently on Synth, MIDI and CV clips without becoming automation destinations.

    Generate is the one that is not a setting at all — it is a command that rewrites the clip. It has no MIDI command either, so it cannot be fired from outside the instrument; Dice remains the only thing in this group that can.

    Stochastic is the interesting case, and it is an exception in the other direction. Its own two controls are unreachable over MIDI, but the variation it plays is chosen by the shared Dice — which does have a global MIDI command, learnable and stored in the unit rather than the song. So the one generative control you can reach from outside moves two pages at once, and the pitches and the gates change together. Section 09 has the command itself.
